articles.text:
SPECIAL TRADES INTELLIGENCE.

CO-OPERA.TION VE 'RS US TRADE
UNIONISM..

IT is with the deepest regret we notice
this week the proceedings of the annual general
meeting of the shareholders of the Whitwood
Collieries Company. lithe Messrs. BRIGGS had
formed their so-called co-operative company for
the purpose of inflicting the deepest possible
injury on the cause of co-operation, they could
not have adopted a more certain means of
producing such a result than by proposing and
passing the resolution against trades unionism
they succeeded in carrying at their annual
meeting of shareholders on Monday, the 19th
inst.

There is no necessity to go into the argument
as to whether trades unions or co-operative
sooieties are calculated to do most permanent
good. to the working people. It would be
worse than idle to discuss an abstract question,
which must, in the end, be settled by facts
and not by arguments. Those who have
given most time to the study of the working
man's condition, and who have sought most
earnestly for practical remedies, with a view
to its improvement, whatever else they may
have differed about, have agreed most thoroughly
in the belief that, next to wise thought and
sound practical aims, the great thing to be
desired is the avoidance of those antagonisms
by which the people's strength has been at all
times so lamentably wasted. We have now in
Great Britain two mighty forces—the co-
operative and trades unionist, two huge
moving bodies full of vitality, each in its own
way struggling for the improvement of the
condition of the masses of the people. In
friendly alliance, almost every possible good
in connection with the social and industrial
life of the nation becomes attainable. In
antagonism, the worst evils may be de-
veloped, and, above all things, the emancipa-
tion of the wage-receiving class, by such a
hostility, may be indefinitely postponed. Mr.
ARCHIBALD BRIGGS and his shareholders seem
to have taken upon themselves this most
undesirable work. Without cause, certainly
without suflicient cause, they have placed co-
operation in antagonism with the trades
unions of the country, and, by so doing, have
put upon the friends of co-operation the duty
of vindicating their principles from the stigma
such a proceeding is calculated to 1 1 x on them.
In arguing this matter, we must not forget
the old hostility of Mr. BRIGGS to trades
unions. The writer of this article visited
Rothwell-conunon, where men, women, And
children, driven from their homes during a

non-shareholding workmen not possessed by
any other employer of labour in the country.
Nobody could wish to place him in a worse
position as to the control of the works it is
his duty to manage; but if he is to be privileged
to say to the men in his employment that he
will either discharge or in any other way at-
tempt to coerce them for joining a trades union,
every other employer in Yorkshire and else-
where may do the same thing, and if all did
this in hostility to trades unions, we should
have the industry of this country at once
brought to a standstill; and, viiiat is worse,
we should have a social and industrial war
fiercely waged all over the country.
The absolute silliness of what was urged
against trades unions by Mr. BRIGGS and those
who supported him:at the shareholders' meet-
ing,.calls for no refutation. If the co-opera-
tive system—when established in its integrity
—be better than trades unionism, facts and
not logic will make it clear in• time to all
who arc interested. There was nothing urged
by the speakers against trades unionism which
has not been urged over and over again by
its opponents, and which has not been refuted
again and again by those who believe in it
as a great enfranchising and elevating power;
and if it has not been refuted its non-
effect has proved the utter uselessness of
such talk.

Mr. Barons admits that he himself, as
representing his company, is a member of an
employers' union; but he declares, in exten-
uation of this, that he only took part in its
proceedings to regulate the price of coal, and
to watch business !dative to. the alteration
of the law as to the regulation and working
of mines. \Then wages have to be discussed
he leaves the room. How this association
regulates the price of coal the publics have, at
the present moment, an opportunity of
judging. How it superintends the making
of laws for the regulation of mines, working
colliers possess an expensive and saddening
experience. But, whatever the effect of this
master miners' combination, if the men were
to take it into their heads to declare outlawry
against every employer who joined it, as Mr.
BUMS has declared it against his men, we
should very soon find an outcry raised against
such tyranny which it would be difficult to
withstand.

The co-operators of the kingdom should,
as a simple matter of duty to themselves and
their principle, take up this question. It is
not for them to sanction a new thraldom for
labour—to give countenance to an attempt to
impose a yoke almost as oppressive as that
from which working men by their unions are
seeking to escape—flavoured by the old hate-
ful feudal tyranny which has been considered
so long dead. It may be that co-operation,
in the full development of the justice it
embodies, may leave no standing-room for
trades 'unionism ; but that is not the
state of things at the present moment.
There is not only space for both to
operate in, but there is a necessity for
the operations of both. Co-operation, per-
fect as an idea, is simply experimental Its a
living fact. It is seeking to develop° itself in
the work of production in the truest and best
way in the interest of capital and labour con-
jointly. The Bums' collierie.s are simply
one form of this experiment, and by no means
the highest or most hopeful.
.Nevertheless
much good may corns from this if those en-
gaged in it do not fall out by the way, antl

through personal prejudice and mistaken self-
interest sacrifice the principle which we trust
they are honestly seeking to serve. Trades
unionism, on the contrary, is not an experi-
ment. It is an understood power operating
for definite objects. It holds the eggressiVe
force of capital as against labour in cheek, ana
asserts with method and power of enforcement
the claims of labour against capital. Of
course we do not lose sight of the illimitable
twaddle that has been, and is still talked about
"demand. and supply" settling the price of
labour, but we are not to be cheated out of
our consciousness, derived from a long and in-
timate acquaintance with their operations, that
trades unions do give a fuller independence
and ampler means to the operative. They
form a grand fighting wing of the great army
of progress, wide!' by discipline and courage
holds the enemy in check %%Mist the co-
operators are out in advance making their ex-
periments on the new ground where the
foundations arc to be laid, and the superstruc-
ture raised. of a grand and noble fabric of
society in which provision will be made for
the happiness of all. This grand work must
not, in the name of co-operation, be interfered
with by Mr. Dumas. ;rho battle gauge he has
in his anger thrown down to:the unionists
they need. not take up. The co-operators
themselves will kick it out of the way, and
join with them in laughing at the futile
attempt made to divide the two bodies of
working brethren, who have, as yet, given the
highest assurances of success in their efforts
for a wise and peaceable emancipation of
labour equitable to all classes, and therefore in
the highest degree desirable in the interest of
the nation.
Right and Duly are like two palm trees,—unless they grow together thty bear no fruit.

articles.text:
THE AGITATOR.

I inc you will permit me to correct a mis-
print which occurs in my letter addressed to
Mr, GEORGE MITCHELL, published in your last
number under " Agricultural Labourers'
News."

I did not say that " agitation" is the spi-
ritual agent of all modern progressive move-
ment, but that the "agitator " is so ;
meaning that, while in former times it was the
priest who was constanqy calling men •to a
higher life, it is the much-abused " agitator"
who does so now. Of course there may be
self-seeking agitators, who aro unworthy of
the cause they profess to represent, as there
have been priests unworthy of their mission ;
but, in the main, I believe it will be found that
those who agitate on behalf of the oppressed
poor, and against the tyrannical circumstances
created and maintained by either selfish or
thoughtless well-to-do people, exercise, like
Mr. GEORGE *ITCIIELL, a spiritual force for
geed, and are, liko him, honest, conscientious,
and worthy of our highest regard.

I am prepared to sssert, moreover, in
spite of ignorant class declamation, whether
on tho part of bishop or duke, that the agi-
tator on behalf of the poor, unlike the agitator
ou behalf of the wealthy, is commonly a
personal loser by his agitation.

FREDK. A. MAXSE.

MR. HARRISON'S PROPOSAL FOR THE

DOUBLE SHIFT.

Mn. IlsnnisoN's recommendation of Mr.
BRASSEY'S suggestion, for working double
shifts of eight hours each, contained in your
issue of the 10th inst., will, I have no doubt,
receive that attention which every word from
the pen of that gentleman merits; therefore,
though I have, as yet, seen no notice taken of
the Suggestion, I have no doubt that what
has been said has entered deep into many
thoughtful minds, and that a fuller discussion
of it would prove serviceable.
The proposal is to introduce into all
industries, where machinery largely assists
the work of production, a double day, of 16
hours, the men being, on the double-shift
system, employed 8 hours per day.
.This plan would enable the employer, in
every 24 hours, to get nearly doubt° the
work which he now gets out of his capital
sunk on buildiUgs, machinery find toolc ile
would also turn over his circulating capital
(required for 'materials, wages, '&0.) nearly
twice, where he now turns it over but -once.
These advantages would induce him to think
highly of what he might lose by having to pay
a day's wages for 8 instead of oor 10 hours
work,

The system would, of course, only apply to
work done in well-lighted buildings, or in
inirum, and would thdefore be applicable only
to a minority of the working olasSes.
Whether the practical inconveniences arising
to men, women, and children, from having
either to commence work as early as '5.30 a.m., or
to leave oir as late as 9.30 p.m., would outweigh
the advantages of a shorter day must be
decided by each individual. The chief points
which we have to discuss are, the effect of a
largely increased supply of goods upon the
markets, and the influence upon labour of
such a change being carried out to the full
extent of its applicability. Let us examine
the latter first.

To carry out, in all mills and factories
now in work, the double shift system,
would require double the number of hands
employed in those industries, This would
absorb not only all the unemployed in
the manufacturing districts, but also all
the idle all over the country. It ought
also to empty the workhouses of all the
Able-bodied inmates, and would give society,
whenever the iuendioant was caught begging,
to "know the reason why." Such a revolu-
tion would only be worked out gradually,
at first by a few of the younger and more en-
terprising manufacturer, but after once the
ice had been broken, the rest would follow with
daily increwsing rapidity, If, after disous-

slop, the proposal should be deemed sound,
it would be well worth the while of those
mills which are owned and worked on the oo-
operative system to take The lead in the move-
ment. _ _

A change of this kind would not only absorb
all the surplus labour, but would also cause a
considerable and general rise in wages. This
increase might perhaps swallow up .the extra
profit the manufacturers would extract from
the fuller employment of his machinery, Sze.,
and yet he would double his previous proats,
by doubling his power of production..
Increased employment, heeompanied by
improved wages, would be folloiied.- by such
an increased demand for food, clothing, &0.,
as Would g 6 fai towards taking to- the Whole
of the incroa,secl supply, and as the change
would be by no means instantaneous, the
additional supply would be pi:ovicled for by
increased. nonsumption in the foreign and
colonial markets.

I hope these hastily written thoughts will
aid the important discussion.

WILLIAAL H. LArltD.

articles.title: WORKMEN'S CITIES.*
articles.text:
WORKMEN'S CITIES.*

IT is gratifying to the more advanced social
reformers to see that so much progress has
been made in the idea of the reconstruction of
Our social arrangements, as is indicated by
the founding of the "Workmen's City,"
which was practically commenced by the
Earl of SIIAFI ESBURY On the third of the pre-
sent month. But it we are .to judge of the
ideas of the founders of this new city as to
what is needed •to effectually ameliorate the
condition of the working classes, from the ad-
dress of the respected nobleman who officiated
upon this interesting occasion, and from the
proposed arrangements, these social reformers
have still 'much to learn. It is much that
well constructed cottages are to be put within
the reach of the working man who is well
employed at decent -wages.; and schools, and
co-operative stores, and reading rooms, and
pleasure grounds, &c. But a great deal more
must be done before the position of the work-
man will be made satisfactory. The fully
organized workmen's city must contain all
these things; hut it must also possess the
means to 'provide permanent and well re-
munerated employment for its inllbitants,
and to give to their children an ethication by
which the physical constitution, the intellectual
powers, the moral nature, and the practical
capabilities of every fairly organized child
shall be really well developed—by which all
shall be caused to acquire a character of true
englightenrcent and. enlightened goodness, and
of great practical usefulness.
To provide this permanent eniployment, the
production and dihtribution of wealth must be
organized and regulated within these new
arrangements, in accordance with the principles
of the co-operative social system., and the new
cities must possess the means—in land,
manufactories, &I.—which are necessary to
enable their inhabitants to be self-supporting.
While the working man's income is subject
to the contingencies of the competitive system,
there must always be very many who are
unable to purchasa the advantages of the
new cities, and the subsistence of all must be
more or less pro:milieus. And as long as there
are inequalities of educational advantages,
and. inequalities of general condition, except
those which are appropriate to differences of
age, the positions of all must be extremely
unsatisfactory. There cannot be the mutual
good feeling, and the reciprocal co-operation
for the good of all, which are necessary for
the satisfaction of man's social nature, while
men desire anti endeavour' to obtain advan-
tages or privileges from which others are
excluded. While it is impossible, as it must
be in the present system, that the reasonable
wants of every individual should be plentifully
supplied, and, while men's character is adapted
to this system of selfishness, and disunion,
and mutual opposition, men must, of course,
continue to desire to possess more than is
npossesded by their follow-men; they cannot be
taught by any amount of exhortation to
love their neighbour as themselves, and to do
to others in allthings as they would have others
to do to them. But, when man's character has
been formed under the influences of 'the co-

operative system,..or under the influence of the
knowledge upon which this system is based,
it will he as natural that hi g ideas, and feel-
ings, and conduct, shall be hi harmony with
these precepts, in which the spontaneous
dictates of our moral (or social) nature are
verbally expressed, as that he should desire
his own happinessOr the happiness of his wife
and children. AU the objections which are
made to a system of equality of educational
advantages, &0., are the effects of ignorance
arid selfishness. IVhile men are ignorant of
the primary causes of eVil and of good to man,
and of the co-operative system, and while
they haVe the selfish desires which are the
natural eflets (and also the causes) of
,the
system of dis-uniod and mutual' opposition,
they clarinet know or feel that these inequali•
ties will never form part of a state of things
in which man's moral nature will be rightly
developed, and in which men will know and
will realise practically what is most conducive
to their own happiness its • well ,as to the
happiness of their fellow-beings.
And to provide the education by which
alone the intellect and the moral nature of ell
can be rightly developed from birth, the
schools -within the new cities must be organized
and conducted, and the homes of the children
must be regulated, and all the social influences
by which they are surrounded must be con-
structed, under the guidance and influence of
the knowledge of the causes of evil and Of
good, and of goodness enlightened -by this
knowledge. While this knowledge is not
possessed by the inhabitants of the riew Cities,
and not even by their •leaders, or instructors,
or by the committees by which their social
affairs are regulated, and while the dis-union
and. mutual opposition, and. external inequali-
ties of the present system are maintained
within them, the children can never be well
educated in any schools which can be estab-
lished,-and the general state of their in-
habitants must be very far from satisfactory.
Nothing but the want of this knowledge,.
and the 'want of the enlightened goodness
which this knOwledge alone can produce; now
Prevents the immediate commencement of
these .fully 'organized and wisely conducted
Workmen's Cities, and their extension over
the country, and throughout the world, until
all who are now peer, and ill-placed, and ill.-
edueated, and ill:•cmployed, shall have the
option of entering -Upon a new life in. MAO;
the national happiness of every individual
will be promoted to the utmost possible extent.
These new cities' will be established as easily
as the imperfect arrangement which was in-
augurated by the Earl of SHAFTESIATILY will
be constructed, when the knowledge of this
subject is suffi. eiently disseminated, and no
one who has acquired the spirit of this know-
ledge will be content with any improvements
in our social arrangements in which the
general conditions of the co-operative social
system are not fully realised. See my little
tract on "The Coming Revolution," adver-
tised on page 8. -

JOTTINGS OP A DEPUTATION TO
LANCASHIRE.

-

• Business now calls us to Temperly. Oh, let me
live and dip in Temperley, rural and salubrious;
hero is*a i)aradise for retired carpenters. Evil
the cows graiing•at the sides of its fragrant lanes
turn enquiringly their clean and intelligent faces
as we pass; it soon becomes evident, however, that,
we are the subjects of a suspicious criticism, and a
remark as we pass some young ladies, scarcely
entering their teens, convinces us that your depu-
tation, with their black bags, are looked upon as
itinerent dealers in drapery.
What a pity the Brown Bear has not a toloscopu
powerful enough to follow the wanderings and
aifticultie? of our mission. Terrible long miles aro
those over which we tread to our destination at
Altrincham ; we are amply rewarded, however, on
reaching there by the hearty reception we meet
with, and the practical sympathy extended to our
cause; here, as at many other publichouses, WO
find the following quaint advice framed and bung
in a conspicuous place
FRIENDLY MICE.
Call frequAntly.
' • . Drink moderately.,
Pay honourably.
Be good company.
Part friendly.
Go home quietly.
Let these lines be no man's sorrow,
Pay to-day, and trust to-morrow.

We next visit tho town of Stockport, remark-
able for its peculiar situation. Surely in ages :
past here must have been the scene of some vol-
canic convulsion, for so many ups and downs are
there in its streets that the foUndations of some
houses are on a level with the chimney pots of.
others in the adjoining thoroughfares. Whoever
selected this spot for a town must have had more
regard for the picturesque than the convenience of
its inhabitants. A thriving and extensive town,
however, is Stockport, and on the whole very
pleasanily situated, possessing some very largo
linen and other, factories. Women aro here said
to be in the pidpoition of seven to one man.
A splendid piece of brickwork adorns the
town, such as would do any skilled bricklayer's
heart good to look upon. The superb back
arches which consititute the lino long
viaduct across the Mersey, and over which
tbo London and North-Western Railway
traverses, is a model of skilled workmanship.
After successfully transacting our business here,
wø leave for a town of national and perhaps of
world-wide interest—a town which has attracted
the attention of statesmen and philosophers, and
men of all grades who seek a solution of the great
incubus of modern society—the labour question.
We pass on our route, at intervals, the chimneY
shaft and double wheels, which indicate that
underneath the men are actively burrowing for
the domestic black diamonds, audnear by stand the
low squatty dwellings of the miners, having the
outward appearance of denizens of some subter-
ranean kingdom.
The visitor to Lancashire can hardly fail to
notice some distinctive characteristic of its
people.

Their unostentatious character, the absence of
false delicacy and pride, their industry and
thriftiness, the mutual regard for each others'
welfare, are some of these. There are two great
principles, however, at work in Lancashire, par-
ticularly interesting to workmen, viz., trades
unionism, and its younger brother, co-operation.
At the busy. town ef Rochdale, where we have
now arrived, these are in active and constant
operation. In most Lancashire towns there is a
goodly sprinkling of the 00-operative prinniple,
but nowhere to the extent which exists in Iteeh"
dale. Here the-principle is very largely applied
to manufacture as well as to distribution, ella
immense blocks of buildings are shown to to
which belong to the co-operators, of tho town.
Into the various phases of the question and tho
criticisms to which it has .been subject of late
years, it is not necessary here to enter. Sufficient
be the fact, that the great mass of the workpeople
of the town are connected with one or other of it
great co-operative concerns. The °Seers of the
trade societies we visit are all co-operators, and this
is the feature with which we are more ospechalY
-interested. The workmen of Lancashire et°,
probably, the most thoroughly organized of of
part of the world: There is scarcely a town in
which trades unionists do not largely predomitiate:
and in some towns of twenty to thirty tbousansa•
inhabitants, non-unionists may be 00unte4 °a
one's angers.

Major German has accepted tho invitation
to come forward for Preston in the Libeol
interest.

LONDON.
TILE GAILI*ENT AYERS.
The above trade hold a meeting at the Cam-
bridge Hall, Newman street, on Tuesday, to take
into consideration the best means of shortening
the hours of labour. All branches of the trade
were well represented, and a resolution was
adopted to commence a movement to reduce 'the
hours of labour in the trade.

NOTTINGHAM.
TUE ENGINEERING TRADE.

The non-society men belonging to the engineer-
ing and machinists' trades of Nottingham appear
to be disaffected, and have held an aggregate
meeting in the Assembly Rooms to take into con-
sideration their position with regard to an advance
of 2s. per week on their prerent rate a wages,
which had been demanded by the Amalgamated
Society of Engineers on behalf of its members in
the town. In most shops separate deputations of
non-society men had waited on their employers,
and had, with few exceptions, been met in a very
liberal manner. The meeting unanimously
resolved, "as the interests of non-society men
were in an unfavourable and dangerous position,
and as a very powerful society had been formed
by the principal employers in the town," to form
a new society on a more liberal and leas exolusive
basis than the one already existing, to which all
branches of the trade can be admitted on a more
equitable footing. The society has been called
the Independent Order of Engineers and Machinists
a large number have joined it, and branches are
being formed in other towns.

DARLINGTON.
MALGSMATEn CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.
A picnic to Darlington took place on the 20th of
August, of the Tyne and Wear branches of the
Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners,
comprising Newcastle, Gateshead, Jarrow, Wall-
send, North and South Shields, and Sunderland
branches. The members of the above, along with
their wives, families,, sweethearts, and friends, and
accompanied by the band of the Wellesley Training
Ship, and numbering about 400, were received at
the station by the members of the Darlington
branch: They proceeded to the grounds of Mr.
Spark; which watt kindly; granted for the occasion,
where dancing, cricketing, and other amusements
were engaged in, and a pleasant day was spent.
Mr. Sadler, chairman of the London Carpenters
and Joiners' Short Time Movement, arrived in the
town during the day, and addressed a meeting in the
park fora short time, and to the credit of a body of
trades unionists not a drunken man was to be seen.
They returned home in the evening after a pleasant
day had been spent, and much gratified with the
reception they had received from their brother
members in Darlington, proving, beyond a doubt,
the benefits of unity.

nu,Low Wontotaisr,—l am requested to inform
you, threugh our Committee, that we have estab-
lished a trade union for the better regulation and
condition of our trade. We have made out a list
of prices, and have presented it to our employers:
they have refused to accept them, and have offered

being determined to enforce our demands, have
drawn out a firm: the consequence is they have

of nine firms that agreed to pay our list price; so
that we have a large number of men on our hands
with scarcely any funds to fall back upon, and we
are under the necessity of appealing to our fellow

and some support from our town, but we require
a little more, as our numbers are large, amounting

ing the battle of right against might. It is your

The following address has been sent to ti-e
masters of the above trade :
Gentlemeo,—We, the operative dressers, dyers,
and finishers of Manchester, Salford, and neigh-

hourhood, gratefully mindful of the favours you
have so generously conferred upon us—firstly, by

remuneration for time worked beycnd the ordi-
nary hours of lal‘our, and secondly, for your

cession at your hands.

Under these circumstances, after maturely con-
sidering the subject, we deferentially suggest that
our time of working should be reduced from 59 to
54 hours per week. We are fully sensible that
such a change will necessitate an alteration of
your chaigeslo manufacturers, and to enable you
to effect this vie are desirous to give the utmost
latitude.

A deputation of your own hands will be glad to
have an opportunity of waiting upon you on or
about the 21st October next, to support the jus-
tice of their claim, and to agreo upon the time it
will, suit your convenience for the change to come
into operation.--We are, gentlemen, on behalf of
the operatives, yours respectfully,

XISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.

LoNnow.—Ou Sunday evening one of a series of
meetings of shop assistants of all trades was held
at the Foresters' Hall, Wilderness-row, called
by the Metropolitan Shopkeepers' Assistants'
Association, established a few months ago for the
purpose of obtaining a reduction in the working
hours in retail establishments. The meeting at
first was not very numerously attended, but, the
audience increased considerably before the close.
Mr. George Linnams Tianks presided, and several
addresses were delivered showing how assistants
inshops in every trade were subjected to service
for very long hours, and this at a time when
artisans were laying down the principle of nine
hours' labour as a maximum.

KIILKCALDY.—TIIO striko among tho operative
bootmakers and shoemakers in Kirkcaldy was
brought to a close by the employers granting the
demands of the men, and increasing
.their wages
from lo to 30 per cont. according to the quality of
the work.

FIFIL—Tho miners of Fife and Clackmannan
have been promised an advance of wages equivalent
to 10s. 6d. per week, being the amount of their
last demand. Another largo rise in the price of
coal is considered imminent.

DUBLIN.-1 conference took place on Tuesday
between Sir John Gray, Alderman Purdon, and
Mr. James Scott, of the Dublin _Evening Mail, as
negoelators on behalf of the operative bakers, on
the one side, and:some of the leading master bakers
on the other, with a view to a settlement of the
differences between the masters and men. The
conference resulted iu the making of arrangements
for the resumption of work in a very large num-
ber of the chief bakehouses in Dublin. The strike
is considered virtually at an end.

BIRKENUEAD. - On Monday afternood the
various firms of shipbuilders in Liverpool and
Birkenhead agreed to a general lock out of their
workmen. It is expected, however, that the men
will return to work on the masters' terms, viz.,
2s. per week advance. The master engineers will
also lock out 'those men who decline the proffered
2s. advance. All have gone in but the members of
the Amalgamated Engineers' Society, who stand
out for 10 per cent.
AIA.NCILESTEII.—TIIe tobacco-pipe operatives of
Manchester have received notice from Mr. Therese
Holland, one of the employers, that it is his in-
tention to give the advance of 18 per cent. in
wages, commencing on the 24th inst.
HYDE.—On Wednesday evening the president
and Itecretary of the Manchester and Salford
Trades Council attOnded meeting respectively of

the employers and. operatives at Denton, and
succeeded in bringing about an arrangement for
the appointment of six on each side to act as a
board of conciliation, ivith the president and
secretary of the Trades Council as mediators.

A shark five feet and a half in length was
on Wednesday caught oft' Southampton Pier.

TERMINATION OF DISPUTE
IN THE LONDON '
BUILD-
ING TRADES.

TERMS OF SETTLEMENT.

The conference of the carpenters' deputatien
with the masters was held on Tuesday afternoon j
at Westminster Chambers, Victoria-street, at t3P
o'clock, and lasted till eight o'clock; Mr. 13.
Hannon in the chair. The following mem-
bers of the sub-committee of the Central
A.ssociation of the Master Builders were present:
--Messrs. Brass, Shaw, Macey, Trollop°, with Mr.
Stanley Bird, hon. secretary. The deputation of j
the central committee of the carpenters and
joiners consisted of the following members :
Messrs. Greedy, Mortimer, Burgess, and Whaley,
with Mr. Matkin, secretary. After some preli-
minary discussion, a long debate commenced on the
code of working rules, which were exhaustively
gone over and disputed point by point. No hitch
took place to disturb the tenor of the discussion
until nearly seven o'clock, when two of the
primary points had been settled.
At this stage of the proceedings the deputation
asked to retire for a quarter of an hour to consult
with their committee, who were sitting in the
vicinity. When the deputation consulted the
committee as to the terms of the proposed agree-
ment, certain propositions were moved as to
their acceptance or rejection, and a vote was
eventually carried that the terms should be
accepted. The deputation again met the masters,
and after another hour's deliberation the follow-
ing agreement was come to

- -
2, Westminster Chambers, Angust 27th.
The working hours to be 52i all the year round
for joiners in shops, and 52i hours per week for
40 weeks in summer, and 48 hours per week in
winter for indoor work, leaving off at one o'clock
on Saturday, during winter weeks.
The wages to be 80. per hour all the year
round. _

Outside, beyond the above hours, when worked
at thd request of the employer, to be paid at the
following rates :—For the first hour 91d. per
hour, and from the end of the first extra hour
until eight o'clock, p.m. at the rate of 101 d. per
hour, after eight o'clock at the rate of Is. 0/d. per
hour.

This scale not to apply to the case of men
working overtime at their own request, or to make
up time lost by them during the week. Extra time
on Saturdays to be paid for at the rate of time and
a quarter up to five o'clock, and after that time at
the rate of time and a half.
(Signed) CHAT/LIM Afxrktzt, Secretary,
Carpenters and Joiners.

The following resolution was moved by Arr.
Hannon, seconded by Mr. Matkin, and carried
unanimously
In the opinion of the sub-committoo of the
Master Builders' Association and the deputation
of the carpenters and joiners now met together,
it is desirable that an endeavour should be made
to settle all future questions which may arise
on trade matters by conference or by arbitration.

During the sitting of the conference all the
afternoon groups of carpenters and joinars were to
be seen ia the vicinity of Westminster Abbey and
Victoria-street in animated discussion, or passing
up and down outside the Chambers, anxiously
waiting to hear the result. The majority seemed
anxious that a settlement should be arrived at.
After the conference ended the deputation, along

with the committee, proceeded to the Brown Bear,
Bloomsbury, where a committee meeting was held
to take into consideration the settlement arrived
at. •

After some discussion it was agreed that a
delegate meeting be convened to confirm the settle-
ment arrived at.

On Wednesday evening, a crowded meeting of
the carpentera' and joiners' nine-hour delegation
WaB held- at the Brown Bear, Broad-street,
Bloomsbury, Mr. Thomas Sadler in the chair, to
receive the report of the deputation who waited
upon the Masters' Committee on Tuesday last.
About 160 delegates were present, and much ext
citement prevailed.
Mr. Burgess, a member of the deputation, at
some length detailed the proceedings which had
occurred at the meeting between the deputation
and the Master's Committee. The result was the
adoption of the above agreement. They were the
best terms that could be obtained, and although they
fell short of what they desired, they were a decided
step in advance. He strongly advised their ac-
ceptance by the delegates.
Messrs. Greedy, Whaley, Mortimer, and Mitch-
toy, the ether members of the deputation, cor-
roborated Mr. Burgess.
Mr. Benny then moved the Ldlowing resolu-
tion:—

That this meeting of delegates of the carpenters
and joiners of London, having heard the reports
of their deputation elected to confer with the
Master Builders' Committee upon the existing
points of the dispute' hereby agree to recommend
that work be resumed on the terms agreed upon
between the deputation and the committee of

aSterd: —At IVeFliitif time we further recommend
the continuance of this organization with h view
of obtaining terms more satisfactory to the track,
at the earliest opportunity, and also for tbe purpose
of establishing the terms now agreed upon
throughont the London trade.
Mr. Sinclair seconded the resolution.

Mr. Panchen contended that the terms wore
most unsatisfactory. They had not obtained their
great want—a code of working rules. He only
accepted the terms under protest.
After a long discussion, the resolution was
adopted with eight dissentients.
The following resolutions wore also adopted :
That after Monday, September 2, two members
of the committee shall act in conjunction with the
treasurer and secretary in transacting all business
connected with the movement up to the next
delegate meeting, and that all men now signing
at the district committee rooms and not obtaining
employment before Tuesday, September 3, shall
from that date sign at the Brown Bear.
That the 3s. levy be paid on Saturday as usual,
and that a levy of ls. be paid on saturday,
September 7, until further arFangements are decided
upon.
That the next delegate meeting be held on
Thursday evening, September 6.
After some further routine and general business,
the meeting adjourned.

VIE OLD AND NEW Tgams.
To form a judgment as to what the men have
gained or lost by the compromise, it will be neces-
sary to compare the terms of the agreement
adopted on Tuesday, and the original terxns of the
memorial sent in by the men.
The men, in their memorial, claimed that 51
hours should be the working hours per week, at
94. per hour. This would have been a reduction
of the working hours per week by 51 ansl an in-
crease of wages of Id. per hour; but owing to the
reduced hours the actual increase in each man's
wage per week weuld have been 7. only, 56i
hours at 81 per hour producing a weekly wage of
LI 17s. Bd., and 61 hours at 9d. produeing
LI 18s. 3d. By the terms of the compromise they
have accepted 62i hours per week at Bid. per
hour, which produces the weekly wage (excluding
fractions) of £1 17s. 2d., or 6d. per week less than
they are now receiving. The men ha,vo therefore
got the advantage of a reduction in their hours of
labour by four hours per week, with the privilege
of leaving work at 12 o'clock on Saturday, at the
sacrifice of 6d. per week in wages. This is no
doubt a substantial advantage, and the terms are
slightly better upon the whole tiln those obtained
by the masons.

On the second point in their memorial—the code
of working rules, by which they desired to check
the system of overtime and abolish piece-work,
the compromise is unfavourable to them. By the
copy of the proposed code of rules laid before Vie
masters by the deputation, it WAS proposed that
all overtime should be paid for at the rate of time
and a half for the first two hours, or any part
thereof, and double time for every hour afterwards.
Thus, reckoning the wages at Elid. per, hour, over-
time for the first two hours would have been
paid ls. Old. per hour, and every other le. sd.
This price, the men contended, would have the
effect of putting an end to the evil of systematic
overtime. By the terms of the compromise, over:
time is to be paid as follows or one penny
beyond the regular wage, for the first hour; and
at the rate of teid., or nearly time and a quarter,
for the succeeding two hours; and is. Old., or
time and a half, for every following hour. It
will at once he seen that, as regards payment for
overtime, the terms of the compromise fall very
short of the claim made by the men, while the
code of working rules has been altogether ignored.
The dissatisfaction of the men with the com-
promise arises mainly from this cause, and will
probably give rise to a renewed struggle at the
first opportunity. In the meantime the strike of
the carpenters and joiners may be considered as
concluded, and the men, as a body, intend resuming
work this morning. The new terms as to hours
and wages will commence from Saturday next.
On Wednesday morning the bricklayers' depu-
tation met the masters at the Westminster Cham-
bers. The deputation consisted .of six members,
headed by Messrs. Coulson and Batchelor, The
same sub-committee of the masters who sat on
Tuesday were present, with Mr. B. 'Lumen in the
chair. Very little discussion took place. The de-
putation, on being asked if they came fully em-
powered to settle the dispute, Tepliod in the flogs.
tire; at the same time they informed the masters
they were willing to enter into a discussion as to
the terms of a settlement; but as they were not
fully empowered to conclude terms the masters
declined to enter into any debate. The brick.
layers' deputation retired to report to their com-
mittee the result of their interview. If the
bricklayers' committee come to the resolution to

fully empower their deputation 'to effect a settle-
ment, the masters are ready to re-open the ques-
tion. Should no 'agreement be arriveti et by the

close of the week with the bricklayers, the strike
against certain firms will be re-commenced de novo.
The conference of the deputation of the amal-
gamated trades' committee with the masters' com-
mittee took place on Wednesday afternoon at three
o'clock, lasting until six o'clock. The sub-com-
mittee of the Masters' Association came fully pre-
pared for the discussion of the different codes of
rules as affecting each respective trade. The
masters, all through the conference, gave due con-
sideration to every argument advanced, and every
latitude was extended to all the speakers. At the
close of the debate the following agreement was
drawn up and signed on behalf of the trades con-
cerned :

2, Westminster Chambers, August 28.
' The working hours in the shops to be 521 all
the year round, and 524 hours per week for 40
weeks in the summer and 48 hours per week for
out-door works in the winter weeks. Leaving
off work at one o'clock on Saturdays in the winter
weeks. The wages of all the trades represented,
and the labourers, to be raised one halfpenny per
hour above the present rates. The overtime
beyond the above hours, when working at the
request of the employers, to be paid at the
following rates—viz., for the first hour one penny
extra for mechanics, and one halfpenny extra for
labourers. From the end of the first extra hour
up to eight o'clock p.m. at the rate of twopence
for mechanics, and one penny extra for labourers.
After these hours at the rate of time and a half
for mechanics and labourers alike. The extra
time on Saturday to be paid at the rate of time
and a, quarter up to five o'clock, and after that
time at the rate of time and a half.

This scale not to apply to the ease of men
working overtime at their own request, or to make
up time lost by them during the week.
(Signed)
W. L. Purr.urs, Painter.
G. A. Vivi Art, Smith.
P. KENNY, Labourer.
J. SAINSBURY, Plasterer.
GEORGE BRUTON, Painter, Secretary.

It will le seen that the above agreement is
similar to that of the carpenters, except as to the
arrangements as to working overtime. The agree-
ment comes into force on Monday.

The Carpenters awl Joiners' Central Committee
on Monday " struck " the same dividend as last
week, viz., 16s. to Jackson and Shaw's and Brass's
men, and 13s. to the remainder. The number of
recipients was not disclosed.
The bricklayers have issued their second "Lon-
don Strike Report," from which it appears the
cost of the strike,,first report, July 20th, is put
down at 1.02 Bs.; total cost of strike £229 13s. 11d.
The above represents the money paid by the
society. With the addition of the collections the
entire cost up to August 10th, is £466.

The labourers Mho wore withdrawn from Messrs.
Jackson and Shaw's firm received a dividend of
13s. 3d. per man, and their committee report that
funds are flowing in to a largo amount. The
labourers are about calling a great aggregate
meeting of their body, at which a report will ho
read, giving a history of their struggle, and the
position of the London building labourers.

Wednesday's Meeting of the Metropolitan
- Railway Company was of a very animated
character. Sir E. Watkin, in moving the
adoption of the report, proposed also the
appointment of a committee of investigation,
and urged that this body should decide also
upon the number and constitution of the future
Board of Directors. Ile expressed his strong
disinclination to continue as chairman of the
company, but said. that if the proprietors
though it for their interest he should not shrink
from the duty. He still believed the line to he
a fine property, ard that if they would have
the courage to make it sound, and to bestow
upon it hard work, they would in no un-
reasonable time find that they had an invest-
ment of a very valuable nature. In the dis-
cussion which followed attention was drawn to
the past management of the railway, and
notice was particularly directed. to the fact that
for several years the rate of the declared divi-
dend exceeded the per centage of gross earnings.
The report was ultimately adopted, and the
committee appointed, the chairman stating
that ho held the resignations of all the
directors until the committee had made its
report.
A three days' Eisteddfod and Musical'
Festival opened at Portmedoc on Wednesday.
The gathering, so far, is described as having
been an unqualified success.

THE LONDON BAKERS.

On Monday night a crowded meeting of the
master bakers of London took place at Auderton's
Hotel, Fleet-street—Mr. Dwarber in the chair—
to frame and approve a platform of principles
previous to meeting the men in conference, and
also to elect 18 delegates to meet the men in such
conference. Nearly every district of London was
represented, and some hundreds of masters were
present.
Mr. E. S. Mantz, the s ecretary of the Trades
Protection Society, gave a detailed statement of
the circumstances which had led to the presen
meeting.

The -Chairman said the meeting was called to
discuss certain resolutions which had been laid
before them by the committee of the Protection
Society, and he trusted they would approach the
question in a spirit of whole-heartedness, and
with a determination that from that time forth
something should be done to better the condition
of the trade at large.
The first proposition was then laid before the
meeting, and was 118 follows—

That a working day shall consist of twelve
hours, and not to oommenco before four o'clock in
the morning.
Mr. Bonthem then moved an amendment—

That a working day shall consist of twelve
hours a day and 72 hours per week, but that such
twelve hours be left to the requirements of each
particular shop.
A discussion ensued, which lasted for a consider-
able time.

The Chairman then put the amendment to the
meeting, when it was declared carried by a large
majority, about a dozen hands being held up for
the original motion.
The next proposition was—
That the committee see no means of abolishing
Sunday bakings except by act of parliament.
Mr. Hollis moved and Mr. Compton seconded
the resolution, which was carried by a large
majority after some discussion.

articles.title: Mitchell moved the third proposition—
articles.text:
Mitchell moved the third proposition—

That as a principle it may be correct that 33. per
week should be added to the wages of the mon,
yet as the wages paid are so various it is desirable
that we have more definite information laid
before us.

Mr. Bonthom seconded, and after some discus-
sion it was declared carried.

The fourth proposition was—

That sack, yeast money, flour, bread, and all
other perquisites be abolished, and the wages of
the operatives be raised according to their value.
Mr. Hollis proposed, and Mr. Brod() seconded.

The question of overtime was then brought
before the meeting, and it was agreed that by
fixing the time at 72 hours per week the meeting
had virtually allowed overtime to exist. The
consideration of the overtime question was there-
fore postponed. The meeting then proceded to
elect 18 delegates to represent the masters at tho
proposed conference.
The proceedings terminated at a late hour of
the evening by a vtoe of thanks to the chairman.
The meeting of masters has led to serious
matters. A strike in the London baking trade is
now apparently only a question of time, the
masters having, at their meeting on Monday,
rejected the 1 to 1 system, the very foundation and
groundwork of the present agitation. Much irri-
tation has been created among the men by the
principles then laid down, but it is doubtful
whether the masters, as a body, are aware of this
fact. They arranged and discussed the pre-
liminaries of the conference, forgetting that by
passing the first resolution on their paper they had
put it out of the question. While the masters
were bolding their meeting at Anderton's Hotel,
the delegation elected to represent the men held a
private conference to still further consider, and
amend, if possible, the platform of principles.
The conclusions arrived at were as follows

The 4 to 4 system was considered satisfactory
as a starting point; the abolition of Sunday baking
was not held to be a hard and fast line, but it was
agreed some compromise might be effected. With
regard to the universal rise of 38. per man per
week, and the abolition of the perquisites of the
operatives, the following resolution was passed
That the trade shall recognize a fixed minimum
scale of wages,—viz.' foremen, 30s. ; Scotch
forehands, 265. ; second hands, 21s. ; and third
hands, 215., with the ordinary perquisites.
The proposition that overtime should be paid
for at is., 9d., and 6d. per hour for foremen,
second aud third hands respectively, was retained,
while the following important resolution was
ultimately passed :

That, in the event of the first proposition of
the men's platform being rejected by the masters
at their preliminary meeting, the question of a
conference must be considered at an end, as the
men's delegation have no power to attend any con-
ference or enter upon any discussion unless the
principle of 12 hours—from 4 to 4—stands as the
basis.

The masters not acceding, all hopes of an
amicable settlement are at an end.

The men have an idea of establishing co-opera-
tive bakeries to compete with and undersell the
masters who may be able to continue their
business during the strike. The rough estimate
for the future is as follows :—There are about
13,000 journeymen, about 11,000 being in Union.
It is anticipated that about 6,000 would remain in
work, either by concessions or compromise, while
another 2,000 would emigrate or be sent from
London to jobs. This would leave about 5,000 to
be supported from the strike fund, which would
have to be raised almost entirely by public sub-
scription, the Union having no vested capital to
fall back upon. It is anticipated that considerable
support would be derived from various other
Trades' Unions, and, indeed, promises to that
effect have been made.

On Tuesday evening a very important meeting
of the Central Board of the London Union of
Operative Bakers was held at the offices, King's-
cross; Mr. G. How, president, in the chair.
There was a very largo attendance of delegates,
the room being crowded to excess. Mr. Peter
Pole attended as a deputation fron the Amalga-
mated Board, and laid before the meeting a
resolution which had been passed by the
Amalgamated Board that afternoon. It was to
the following effect
That this meeting of the London Board of the
Amalgamated Union of Operative Bakers suggests
to the Central Board of the London Union that a
day shall positively be fixed by the London
Trades' Council for the operative bakers of London
to come out on strike in consequence of the re-
jection of their demands by the masters, and that
a spirited manifesto be issued by the Trades'
Council, announcing to the public the day of
strike.

This was put to the meeting and approved, and
a resolution to the following effect was ultimately
adopted:—
That this Board will support the Trades' Council
in whatever course they will pursue.

A largo number of operatives addressed the
meeting, and the greatest indignation was evinced
at the manner in which the masters had acted.
Many of those present were strongly in favour of
an i mmediate strike, but this will be decided at
the next meeting of the Trades' Council.
On Wednesday night the London Council met
at the central committee-rooms to consider the
course to be adopted by the journeymen bakers of
London consequent upon the determination arrived
at not to hold a conference at the Central Boards
of the two Unions. Mr. George How occupied
the chair, and there was a largo attendance of
delegates from all parts of London.

A discussion was entered into with regard to
the present situation of affairs, and the first resolu-
tion was moved by Mr. Searle, president of the
Amalgamated Union, and seconded by Mr. How,
president of the London Union, and was to the
following Effect :
That the functions of the delegation shall now
cease in consequence of the resolution passed by
the masters, and that we resign our trust into the
hands of the Trades Council.

This was carried, and the meeting therefore
resolved itself into the usual Council, consisting of
representatives from every branch of the Union.
The next resolution was moved by Mr. E. Adams
and seconded by Mr. Hare, and was as follows:

That the London Trades Council of Operative
Bakers have learnt with feelings of extreme pain
and regret that the Master Bakers' frade Protec-
tion Society have wholly set aside their just and
reasonable platform. As, therefore, no useful
object can be served by a conference, this Council
withdraws its delegation, and leaves with the
masters the responsibility of the situation which
they have created. At the same time this
Council reserves to itself full liberty to adopt such
measures as the interests of the journeymen may
require.

Mr. Harvey said the men of London, obedient
to the masters' wishes, had elected the best men
they could find, and the masters, finding that able
men had been appointed, had given them tlio cold
shoulder. Under those circumstances every dele-
gate should go back to his branch and tell the
state of the matter, and they
_would then be able
to decide on the course to be taken.

Tbe question of a strike was thou taken into
consideration, and after considerable discussion
Mr. Giles said it would be bad policy to strike
in districts, and proposed
That a day shall be positively and definitely
fixed for the journeymen bakers of London to
come out on strike.

Mr. Adams seconded the motion.
Mr. Greenwood believed that if the bakers of
London agreed to a complete strike at a certain time
the masters would b.) bound to come to terms.
(Cheers.)
Mr. Andrews, speaking for the German portion
of the Union, said the whole of the journeymen at
the East-end were quite willing to adhere to the

AUG. 31, 1872.

terms of the first proposition laid down by the
men. (Applause.)
A long discussion ensued. The men almost
unanimously decided that there should be a strike,
and the day was fixed. A "strike committee
was elected, with a chairman and secretary, to
control the actual business of the movement, and
it was determined also that a spirited public
manifesto should be issued calling upon the publio
for assistance and subscriptions.

articles.title: POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH
articles.text:
THE POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH

SERVICE.

The Post-office officials of the minor establish-
ments have, by every legitimate means, ..tried to
obtain an improvement in their position to meet
the increased and still increasing prices of every
necessity; but their earnest and respectful com-
plaints have met with no response from tho"powers
that be," beyond the issue of a "revised scale of
wages" that the authorities have endeavoured to
hoodwink the public to believe is an improvement.
Instead of this being the case, they have, by such
act, only added insult to injury by a deliberate
misrepresentation of the men's position, and closed
up every avenue of promotion to the letter-carriers,
notwithstanding their published promise to those
men, that promotion to other branches of the
service was open to them. Well may the workers
of the nation exclaim is this the Liberal Govern-
ment we are asked to support when each succes-
sive election takes place? But the rulers of this
great national establishment may rest assured that
unless their employes are treated in a more truly
liberal manner, that they will only drive matters
to a crisis which would be disastrous to the nation
at largo. From all parts of the country—north,
east, south, and west—we hoar of nothing but
injustico to all the working staff; from clerks,
sorters, letter-carriers, auxiliaries and assistants,
the cry is the same, town or country alike, and the
pay and treatment of the rural messengers is a
scandal to a professedly Christian and wealthy
country. The whole system of our postal institu-
tion is rotten to the core, and in a state of
smothered rebellion; from this the employes have
no hope of raising themselves but by united action,
and it is during the recess that they should take
such. Clerks, sorters, letter-carriers, and employes
of all grades must unite in one common effort,
sink all class feelings and prejudices, and work
with each other harmoniously for the common
good of each other. They should do as
other bodies of labour if they desire to keep them-
selves from falling lower and lower in the social
scale. Outside aid has been relied on too long;
been well Lied and found wanting. Agitate!
Agitate! Agitate! and success must be obtained
if their demands are just; if not, they deserve to
fail. But agitation without organization is useless,
therefore organization must be the first and only
thought. Let no counsels from would-be friends
deter you from this one object. With the whole
of your forces organized, nothing can withstand
you; as you are, even the agricultural labourers
and washerwomen are leaving you behind, while
you cry out for help, help, where no help is to be
found. When organized, public meeting after
meeting should be held in order to bind you closer
together, and arouse in each other one common
feeling of unity. If you desire redress for your
grievances, your leaders must spring from your-
selves, and those leaders must be supported, aye,
and well too; let that be thoroughly understood,
there must be no falling from your ranks, but you
must show a serried and unbroken front—ono solid
square. Like an army, your generals you most
obey and support to a man if you wish to be Vic-
torious; defeated, and you only sink deeper and
deeper in the mire of "revised scales," without
benefit in alterations, without relief. The time
is coming, and if 'neglected this once, may riot
occur again for years. 'Let your watchword
throughout the whole country be "Unite !"

articles.title: COAL MINERS.
articles.text:
THE COAL MINERS.

TILE EMIT HOURS MOVEMENT.

The eight hours' movement is being vigorously
agitated for by the miners of Notts and Derby-
shire. A great demonstration of colliers has been
made in its favour at Clay-cross. A procession was
formed, a band of music was engaged from Alfre-
ton, and a mass meeting was held in a field, where
addresses were delivered by representatives from
the Butterley, Melton, Devonshire, Silkstone,
Grossmoor, Lings, and Clay-cross collieries. The
chairman, Thomas Moor, of No. I Pit, Clay-cross,
said he considered eight hours a day in a mine was
sufficiently long for any man to work, and that
the proposed reduction would be a benefit rather
than a disadvantage to the employers. The
concession had already been granted in York-
shire.

George Utteridge, a miner, also of Clay-cross,
urged the reduction of the hours of labour as a
means of lengthening the lives of colliers who
suffered greatly from the noxious gases breathed
while in the pit.
Thomas Wheeldon, of Butterley, was in favour
of a graduated scale of payment for coal-winning
If, when the coal was selling at LI a ton, the
miner was paid 2s. 6d., on the coal being raised to
30s. he ought to receive 3s. 9d. at least. Had such
a system been in operation before the recent ad-
vance in coals, they would now be receiving an
Increase of Is. Bd. per ton, instead of about 81d.
Samuel Hancock, of Morton Colliery, in speak-
ing of the eight hours system, said more coa
had been brought to bank since the introduction of
the nine hours system than there had been pre-
viously in the same time. During the past
month the quantity of coals sent to London had
exceeded by 3,000 tons the largest quantity which
had ever been sent before during one month.
There were several other speakers, and ultimately
a Union was formed, to be called the Derbyshire
and Nottinghamshire Miners' Association.
On the following evening a crowded meeting of
miners was convened at Ripley, which was
attended by two partners of the Butterley com-
pany. The meeting had been called because
Wheeldon, one of the speakers at the Clay-cross
gathering, had had to leave his work in conse-
quence of his having advocated the formation of
a Union. The matter was then fully discussed,
and after Mr. Corfield, one of the partners of the
company, had said it would be a serious thing if
they determined to adhere to the Union, as by so
doing they would be going directly contrary to
the wishes of their masters, a motion was pro-
posed that they should leave the Union. It was
not seconded, but a show of hands was then taken
for the Union, when all voted for it except one.

THE BETTY SYSTEM.

The evils of the " butty" system, which are so
common to the Derbyshire and Yorkshire collieries,
have recently manifested themselves in Notting-
hamshire, and on Thursday they culminated in a
strike at the Clifton pits near Nottingham. It ap-
pears that the loaders were greatly dissatisfied
because their wages were notvaised by the " hut-
tymen " in proportion to the advance the latter
had received from the masters; and having been
encouraged by certain " agitators " from York-
shire and Derbyshire, they resolved to strike
work. In consequence of the absence of loaders,
the coal could not be carried to the pit's mouth.
The manager has seen the disaffected men, and
they have been prevailed upon to resume work;
but as they have struck without giving any notice,
the principals in the movement are to be brought
before the magistrates. The proprietor of the
workings, Mr. Saul Isaac, is to meet the under-
ground workmen on MG nday, when it is hoped the
matters in dispute will be amicably arranged.

articles.title: TIIE WAGE QUESTION.
articles.text:
TIIE WAGE QUESTION.

Last week the coal miners employed at the
Swanwiek Collieries, near Alfreton, Derbyshire,
struck for an advance of 4d. per ton on all sorts of
coal. Several large meetings were held, it being
determined to persist in the demand. On Friday
evening the masters said they wore willing to
make an advance of 3d. per ton on the Lard coal,
and 4d. per ton on the soft. At a large meeting
the same night it was resolved, amid loud cheer-
ing, that the men should resume work on the
following morning, leaving their committee to
negotiate with the masters as to the other Id. per
ton on the hard coal. In the event of this not
being conceded there will be another strike.

TIIE SOUTH YORKSIIIRE COALOWNERS AND TIIEIR
MEN.

The demand for an advance of wages to the
extent of 20 per cent. recently made by the colliers
of South Yorkshire, was considered at a very large
meeting of colliery proprietors, held on Tuesday
night, at the King's Head Hotel, Barnsley. Be-
tween thirty and forty collieries were represented,
the chair being occupied by Mr. C. Bartholomew

After the subject had been fully discussed, a depu-
tation of between twenty and thirty men, headed
by Mr. Normansell and Mr. Casey, was ushered
into the room. The question of the advance was
then gone into. On the part of the proprietors an
advance of 15 per cont. was agreed to be given
Mr. Normansell and Mr. Casey said the proposition
would be laid before a meeting of delegates from
the various lodges, which would be specially con-
vened on Friday.
STRIKE AT EARL PITZWILLIAM'S COLLIERY.

About 130 of the " trammers " employed at
Earl Fitz william's Low Stubbin Colliery, near
Rotherham, struck work on Monday morning,
and, in consequence, the whole of the colliers,
packers, and fire-triers, numbering about 180, were
also obliged to cease work. The men state that
five weeks ago an advance of 5 per cent. in prices
was conceded throughout the South Yorkshire
district. This advance has never been fully given
to them, some part being kept back by the master.
They have thereiore struck work, and intend to
remain out until not only are they paid full prices,
but the back money is paid to them.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

ILVESIIANf.

Oa Thursday night a public meeting of agricul.

tural labourers was held on the Merstowe Green;
Mr. Councillor Airey, of Worcester, presided, and
addressed the meeting at some length, advocating
the principles of the union, and entreating the
labourers to join, if they wished to get a fair day's
pay for a fair day's work. Some few years ago
10s. would go farther towards maintaining a family
than Ll at the present time; and yet if the
labourer asked his employer for a rise in wages ho
was told the farmers could not afford it. This
was untrue; for the farmers lived in regal style,
keeping aristocratic establishments and fine
hunters; and if they could efforcl this style of
thing, could they not also afford to pay their
labourers a little better? Messrs. Pill and Rus-
sell, two Warwickshire labourers, afterwards ad-
dressed the meeting. Shortly before the opening
of the meeting, Police-Superintendent Stanton
walked up to Mr. Airey, and gave him a notice,
signed by the Mayor, prohibiting the meeting
being held, and stating that if, after the service
of sudi (g hich was addressed to Messrs.
F. J. Airey, E. Pill, E. Russell, W. Conn, and
others), the meeting was held, "all parties con-
nected with it" would be proceeded against
according to law. Mr. Airey road the notice to
the meeting, and said be was sorry for the Mayor,
who had made himself appear ridiculous by the
proceedings he had taken in the matter.

articles.title: ItUGIIY.
articles.text:
ItUGIIY.

On Monday night, about 1,500 persons, chiefly
farm labourers, assembled in a field at New
lton, adjoining Rugby, to hear Mr. Joseph
Arch on the labourers' movement. A waggon
under a tree served for a platform, and when
darkness sot in candles were brought for this
reporters. It was so dark that the speakers literally
addressed an invisible audience. The meeting was
most enthusiastic.
Mr. J. A. Campbell, a resident landowner, far-
mer, and magistrate, presided, and expressd his
hearty approval of the labourers' movement as
eminently calculated to elevate the condition of the
class of the community. The Union, he said,
had been grossly misrepresented. It was the
result of the tyranny of the farmers in not paying
their men higher wages, which the times de-
manded, but there was nothing in the rules to
tyrannise over the farmers.

Mr. Joseph Arch, the " apostle of the move-
ment," who was received with warm applause,
spoke at great length on various incidents that had
attended the present agitation. In replying to the
Bishop of Gloucester, he remarked that if his
lordship tried to give him a ducking, ho would try
to give his reverence a thorough baptising in
return. If ho could find in the Scriptures that
his Divine Master ever set his foot on the neck of
the poor, then he might sneer at the agitation ;
but one of the apostolic succession, with £5,000 a
year, might have some sympathy for the downs
trodden, and might feel some gratitude toward-
those by whose toil his table was spread with
plenty. (Cheers.) Mr. Arch condemned the
employment of the soldiery in the harvest field as
a scandalous measure, because it was uncalled for,
and only playing into the bands of the farmers.
The labourers, having brought their grievances be-
fore the public in a law-abiding, Christian-like man-
ner, were not going to be put down by the Duke of
Marlborongh, who should remember whence he
got his estate, and that pensions usually died out
with those to whom they were given.
A resolution was carried by acclamation in
favour of the Union, and the usual vote of thanks
concluded the proceedings.

articles.title: MINERS' CONFERENCE IN
articles.text:
MINERS' CONFERENCE IN

GLASGOW.

conference of miners' delegates was held in
Glasgow on Monday, Mr. John M‘Phie, Maryhill,

presiding.
Mr. Alex. M'Donald, minors' secretary, stated
that there was no delegate present from the
county of Fife, but he had received a note from
Mr. Penman, the president of the district board,
authorising him to represent them at the con-
ference. The condition of Fife was this, that they
had over 4,400 persons in the organization. At
the next board meeting, their funds would amount
to upwards of £2,000. During the time the
union had been in existence they had not lost one
single hour in obtaining advances of wages, which
were about as high as in any portion of the
country. Mr. Penman explained to him that, in
virtue of what he had been advising them for
some time, they had been endeavouring to gain the
ear of two employers, so far as to get a board of
arbitration. They had !met the employers, and
the subjects laid before them were that they
should have a board of arbitration, which should
avert the disastrous consequences of a strike; that
they should have their coal weighed at 20 cwts.
per ton, and also that they should have weekly
pays. They submitted a code of rules to the
employers, which were now being printed, with
the view of being 2irculatsd throughout the dis-
trict. The entire county was organized, and the
men were all working eight hours a day.
The Marybill delegate reported that, with the ex-
ception of one work, they had obtained the advance
of Is. per ton. Since the last conference a great
number of the out-lying districts had joined the
union, which now numbered 1,480 members, and
they had about £l,OOO in the bank.
The Baillieston delegates stated that they were
not doing so well in that district as they could
wish. They had between 600 and 700 members on
the roll, and between £7O and £BO in the bank
Their wages at present were 7s. per day, but some
of the works had got the promise that when they
' commenced their next pay it should be Bs. restricted
darg.

The delegate from the lower portion of the
Larkhall district reported that the men were
nearly all in the union. They worked eight hours'
restricted darg of 24 tons, and their general wage
was Bs. per day. The delegate from the higher
part of the Larkhall district stated that the union
had the entire control of the district, with the
exception of one work. Half of the members of
the union had become so within the last three
months, and they had about £lOO of funds.
The East and Mid-Lothian delegate had pleasure
in stating that his constituents were going on
prosperously. They had over 1,600 members in
their union, and upwards of £lOO in the bank.
With a very few exceptions the men in East had
Mid-Lothian were now working 8 hours, and in
several instances they had been doing so for the
last seven years.

The representative from Stirling and Linlithgow
said that they had just now two works on strike,
and their wages ranged from 7s. 6.1. to 6s. 6d.
for working 8 hours.
The West-Calder delegate said the district
union had £2O in the bank; they got a rise of 61
on tho 12th of August, they were to get an addi
tional 6d., which would make their - wages 7s. per
day of 8 hours. The Blantyre delegate reported
that at a meeting held on Wednesday last, 42
names were enrollo I for the purpose of forming a
union. In the ironstone mines their wages at
present were about 9s. per day. The Ayrshire
delegate spoke consenting the position of a great
many pits, and his statement was to the effect that
nothing like uniformity of practice prevailed.
Mr. Alex. McDonald said he could state with
confidence that there were at this moment More
men organized than at any previous period in the
history of this country. Mr. McDonald went on
to speak of the efforts that had been made for a
long series of years to introduce a change in the
legislation with respect to the mining industry.
After twenty-seven years of hard effort and
struggle, they had at last obtained the Mines
Regulation Bill of the present session, which
gave them nearly everything they asked. It was
proposed by the miners in England and Wales that
addresses recognising, the part they had taken in
behalf the miners, should be presented to Mr.
Bruce, Lord Elam, Mr. Mundella, Mr. Brown,
Lord Morley, Lord Shaftesbury., and Lord Ein-
naird, and he suggested that the Scotch miners
might join their English brethren in this move-
ment.

It was resolved that the different unions in
Scotland should join with those of England in
presenting the addresses.

A proposal was adopted that the delegates
should consult with their constituents WI to the

best mode of forming a National Confederation of
Miners, and send in reports to Mr. McDonald
and Mr. Samuel Hughes, who would put the
matter into shape by the next conference.

articles.title: LONDON FANCY CAErrrET
articles.text:
THE LONDON FANCY CAErrrET

MAKERS.

A meeting of fancy cabinet makers was held at
the King's Arms Tavern, Mitchell-street, St.
Luke's, relative to an advance of wages. Mr.
Joseph Boswell occupied the chair.
The Chairman said he thought they should elect
some delegate to have an interview with the
masters.

Mr. Hersey said they were not asking for
more wages. They bad had reductions in wages,
and he called it getting back their former prices.
Ile had had a reduction of wages twice in four
years.

Mr. Dendridge said they continually kept
dropping the prices, but they never advanced them.
There is another subject they should take notice
of, that is the out-door men, of whom therb are
many, have to supply their own glue, brads and
glass papers. They should be allowed for this,
and in addition they saved tho masters the use of
benches.

Mr. Hersey said Mr. Brand had offered to givo
5 per cent. advance on his own account, but ho
wished to see 10 percent. given. ThTs ho said not
out of any antagonism, as be thought it would ho
for the benefit of masters and men.

It was proposed to elect a committee of twflye
members, and an amendment was proposed that a
member of committee should be elected from each
shop.

The amendment was carried.
The folio wing committee members were elected:
—Messrs. Harris, Banbury, Holmes, Pritchard,
Polls, Ellis, Ganett, Mitchell, G. Potts, Grunea.-
gold, T. Potts, Fletcher, Smith, and Marshall.
It was proposed that the:polishers:should likewise
be represented.
It was proposed and carried—

That the committee should meet on Friday and
draw up a memorial for presentation to the
masters, and that they should report to the trade
the result at a meeting to be held on Thursday
fortnight.

After a vote of thank-4 to the Chairman, the pro-
ceedings closed.

articles.title: CONGRESS OF THE INTERNATIONAL WORKING MEN'S SOCIETY.
articles.text:
CONGRESS OF THE INTERNATIONAL
WORKING MEN'S SOCIETY.

The annual Congress of the International,
which last year was omitted in consequence
of military operations in France, will take
place this year at The Hague. The sittings
will commence on Monday next, and will
probably last until the Sunday night follow-
ing. The gentleman who will take the chair
is not yet nominated, it being understoral that
Mr. Jung, who has acted as the President on
former occasions, will not attend the Congress
for certain reasons connected with .the internal
organization of the Society. The delegates of
the general council who have been
wnchasieonsktio,
attend are Messrs. Milner, Ax
Dupont, Conrnet, and SeraHier, and those will
be supposed to govern the whole body. The
representatives of affiliated bodies will be
Messrs. Frankel, Engels, Eecarius, Barry,
Longuet, Ranvier, Johanned, and Val-
liant. Dr. Sexton will also represent an
affiliated body—namely, the Federal Council,
and Mr. Jones, the Manchester section.
Mr. West will attend on behalf of No. 19
American section, whose members advocate
women& rights and views of an extreme
character ; and the delegates from all parts of
' Europe will number one hundred, or more.
It is not yet known what political questions
Will be discussed, or whether the French dele-
gates will bring forward the subject of the
imperial meeting in Berlin as one of grave
importance. In all probability there will be
a long debate on the organization of the
International itself. At present there appears
to be considerable difference of opinion as to
the power vested in the general council,
which, it is asserted by a large number of the
'members, is not of a sufficiently representative
character, and it is likely that an attempt will
be made to re-adjust the misunderstand-
ing now existing between 'Karl Marx and
llakonnine. An endeavour, it is said, will
also be made to organize the Society on a
much stronger and broader basis than here-
tofore.
