Aittitb.

Last Saturday the Spectator printed the follovi-
ing on the t*Heultural labourers' tnovetnent

We confess we look forward to the coming
winter with grave apprehension. We may under-
rate the conservative forces at work— that is always
easy in a country; like_ England—but everything
seems to us to tend towards a social struggle in the
counties which must be disastrous, and may not
be altogether peaceful. The agricultural labourers
of the country, more than 600,000 adult males,
just excited by a new prospect of improved position,
and interested in a now activity, will be exposed
to a new hardship, and irritated by a new form of
pressure from above. Meat, bread, and potatoes
will all alike be dear, and the farmers, en-
riched and emboldenened by their dearness, are
intending, in home counties at all events, to "try
conclusions" with their labourers, and see if they
cannot "read them a lesson " on the advantages
of suffering quietly whatever it may suit em-
ployers to inflict. The prices demanded for getting
in the harvest have irritated the farmers beyond
measure, the speeches of the. itinerant lecturers
often imprud( at, and sometimes most reprehensible
excite them still further, and the sense that in
future they will have to deal with strong corpora-
tions, instead of isolated and therefore powerless
seekers of broad,
,drives them beyond all self-con-
trol, a control which indeed, with dukes and bishops
urging them on, they do not feel it necessary to
retain. The kindly feeling, as they call it, in the
counties—that is the half contemptuous pity on one
side and reverential deference on the other which
has for centuries marked the , semi-feudal relations
of village labour—has already died away, and the
farmers are determined that the men shall know
what " contract "is like. They will not take the
Bishop of Gloucester's advice, and duck the lecturer s
because the labeurers being ten to one, and being
told, by a bishop that physical violence is, a proper
weapon, to employ, might duck the farmers; but
they will jump at tho counsel offered by Mr.
Botheron-Esteourt, a man of blood and mark and
Parliamentary capacity, who advises his three
parishes to treat all who join the 'Union as
"strangers," to withdraw all the perquisites of
which so much is made, to take away the potato-
grounds, to raise the rent of the cottages, and to
refuse to keep on men in winter when work is
wanted. The advice is in the form of a warning
to the labourers, " my friends and neighbours in
Shipton, Newntown, and Ashley ; " but as the
labourers know that without unimi their only
prospects are lives of monotonous toil on wages
insufficient to provide meat, and ending in the
workhouse; as they see that they are abandoned
by the upper class, duke and bishop, and member
and magistrate all alike threatening, scolding, and
warning them; as they see that the half-formed
union has already raised the usual rate of wages
is. 6d, a week, Mr. Estcourt's advice will fall
dead, except upon the farmers. They will endea-
year this winter to put the unions down, and we
shall have all over the country villages in which
ten or fifteen farmers, angry, unreasonable, and
well-fed, will stand face to face with a hundred
and fifty labourers, angry, unreasonable, and
without food. The unionists will be locked out in
heaps, and when they apply to the parish will be
told by the guardians that as they can have work
at will by " merely " giving up the union, they
must take the work.

As we do not in tho least believe in the sub-
missiveness of the British labourer when taken
out of his customary groove—if he takes to the
brickfield, to railway work, or to Australia, he
becomes at once in a day the most brutally
"independent" and personally insufferable of
mankind—as we have a keen recollection of the
way in which the introduction, of machinery was
resisted, when a country-side would be in a glare
night after night and insurances could not be
effected, and, as we believe the labourers in many
districts to have been brooding and champing for
some time past over wildly-dangerous ideas, we
look forward to the struggle with a sickening dread
of the misery it must produce. The English
labourer, once excited, is the most sour of men,
obstinate, scornful, and, for all his horror of blood-
shed, which ie real and rises to a virtue, capable
of being cruel; and he is excited now. The man
has been, so to speak, morally whipped for six
months. Ile has found no friend anywhere
except in a press he can neither read nor under-
stand. The duke has deprived him of his allot-
meat; the bishop has recommended that his
instructor should be ducked; the squire has
threatened him with dismissal in winter; the
magistrate has fined him for quitting work—
which is just —and scolded him for listening to
lectures—which is tyranny; the Mayor, at
Evesham, has prohibited him from meeting on the
Green; and the lawyer—witness a recent case near
Chelmsford—has told him that anyone who advises

him to emigrate is a hopeless rascal. He has
been denied the MOst Ordinary privileges of
freemen—the right of listening to lectures he
approN;es, the right of emigration from county
to country, the right of combining to improve
his condition, and this by men who, as he
sees, listen to every lecturer on their own side,
who emigrate whenever they please to the ends of
the earth, and who form open and strict combina-
tions to keep him in his place. Not one of all
those to whom he ought in county belief to look
up to with reverence has frankly, stood forward on
his behalf. No Peer has gone farther than Lord
Ebury, who advocates a rise of wages, but declares
that combination, which alone can place the
labourer on an equality with his employer,
destroys his " independence," independence
exactly equivalent to the independence of a worm
under a roller,—a right to wriggle at discretion.
No Bishop has come forward to say that Christ's
Church knows nothing of grades or classos„ or
persons with acres, save in so far as it sympathises
most strongly with the humble and oppressed. No
county Member has argued for the freedom of the
non-electors whom he is supposed to represent.
Above all, no statesmen of either aide has deemed
the most-serious social struggle, of our day worth
a speech or even a remark, has attempted to guide
the people, or has so much as endeavoorod to
explain to them the ecenomic laws they are sup-
posed, in some respects rightly supposed, to be
defying. To the labourers, congregating in their
beerhouses and the cottages, talking over the
" agitators' " speeches, and the reports from the
neighbouring villages, and the bitter broadsheets
the respeetables do not see, it must seem as if they
were abandoned by all the world except their own
order. For them it is "the Poor," that endless and
strictly-bound corporation, against the world.
We perceive from the language of the Guardian,
and we perceive it with a deep sense of relief,
that a very considerable section of the clergy are
disposed to take a moderate and conciliatory view
of the movement; to justify the man, and to ac-
knowledge that the feudal system, under which
"men sweat for duty, not for mead," is dying
out; and to deprecate that degrading kind of alms
of which Mr. Estisourt—who would think a gift
of a ton-pound note from a duke a deliberate in-
sult—is so fond; but we fear the clergy scarcely
speak out as frankly as their newspaper does; that
they are unwilling to annoy farmers to whom they
must look for help at the Boards of Guardians;
that the temptation to preach resignation as the
crowning virtue of Christianity overcomes their
knowledge; that resignation is not the virtue by
which civilization is advanced. The labourers in
their own eyes stand alone.
We believe that this is a most dangerous posi-
tion of affairs. Hopeless and hungry Englishmen
are very formidable persons, and if the idea now
prevailing of a look-out of union men in the
winter is carried out, we shall have 150,000 Eng-
lishmen, a fourth of all our labourers, hopeless
and hungry, and filled besides with a sense of the
bitter injustice of all above them, who ask them to
toil twelve hours a day for six days a week, and
then denounce them as wicked for combining to
make their labour as profitable as they em. It is
high time that the statesmen among us, if we
have any who comprehend agricultural ques-
tions, should intervene, and endeavour, if
it may be, to guide and control both
parties, to suggest some terms of coin-
promise, to soothe the bitterness of the farmers,
and above all, to inspire samething of hope in the
masses of the hinds. It is hope they want, if we
are to have continued order in the counties, and
we cannot imagine a higher end to which Mr,
Gladstone's power of sympathetic oratory, or Lord
Derby's hard incisive sense, or Mr. Fertescue's
minute knowledge of all that relates to agricul-
tural tenure, or Mr. Forster's extraordinary faculty
for sympathising with men with whom he does
not agree, could be more,beneficially applied. Let
Mr. Gladstone just inquire into the truth of the
. .
position of affairs in Herefordshire or Oxfordshire
—the real truth, not the truth as squires or
labourers see it—and he will speak out fast enough.
We know perfectly well how hard it will be to
, speak, how great may be the influence of a rash
sentence on the electors, how injurious unfounded
hope must always be; but English labourers are
as deserving of consideration as Irish peasants,
though they do not extort it with the bullet, and
it is time that this reticence and absence of
guidance should come to an end. Let the elec-
tions take care of themselves, and let the poli-
ticians of both sides—for on this subject Tories
are as deeply concerned as Liberals—show us if
they have any wise message to deliver. It is a
strange proof of the unmarked dislocation which
exists in our society, that no trade could full into
confusion without attracting the attention of
ktiteNnen except the most important all. There

was icareely a member in England who did not
deliver hiniself upon the cattle plague, Yet id
presence of an indefinitely greater, of a real and

_ .
permanent scission between employers and em-
ployed, they are all silent, and appeir determined
either to remain so, or to content themselves with
soothing platitudes which, as they perfectly
understand, guide nobody.

VIENNA UNIVERSAL EXHISI-

TION, 1873.

,
Her Majesty's Commission Ora for the Vienna
trnivorsal Exhibition have obtained from the
Director-General of tho Imperial Austrian Com-
mission, Baron von Schwarz-Senborn, answers to
a series of questions of importance to exhibitors
in reference to various details ià conneetion with
the Exhibition, of which the following is a
summary. _

As it is important to assure in time the engines
and steam-boilers intended to set in motion the
machines exhilolted in the English section of the
machinery ball of the said Exhibition, the atten-
tion of English manufacturers is called to this
opportunity to exhibit either fixed steam-boilers,
fixed steam-engines, or portable engines, and also
steam-engines and steam-generators for service in
the machinery hall.

Machinery and apparatus specially adapted to
the requirements of the Exhibition may also be
supplied by exhibitor*, as, for instance :
Boilers for the production of steam for engines.
Steam-engines for driving the main shafting in
the machinery hall,
this and water-power engines, for driving single
machines and groups pf machines.
Large and small pumps for water-works and
fountains,

_
• Travelling cranes, with normal:gauges of 1.5
metre (4 ft. 11 inch from centre to centre), for
service in the machinery hall.

Over-head travelling cranes, with winch and
moving gear, with a gauge a 1013 metres from
rail to rail, for the erection of heavy pieces for the
machinery hall.
Hydraulic lifts for:raising persons. •
Portable engines for the service outside the
machinery hall.
Exhibitors supplying such machines and ap-
paratus intended for special service during the
Exhibition will enjoy
,speoial privileges, to be
arranged between them and the Director-General.

If British makers lend cranes, hoists, boilers
engines, &c., for use of British, exhibitors, no fees
will be levied by the Imperial [Austrian Commis-
sion for the use of the same by I3ritish exhibitors.
But if British exhibitors lend such maehinery for
the use of foreign exhibitors, arrangements will be
made by the Austrian Director-General to indem-
nify British exhibitors for the use of their
muohinery.

The power required to set maohinery and main
shafting for driving machinery in motion will be
supplied by the Austrian Commission, and exhibi-
tors will in no case be charged for motive power
supplied by the main-driving shafts in the
machinery hall.

The moving force will be transmitted by two
horizontal shafts of a diameter of 0.9 metre (about
419 inches), and 120 revolutions per minute is
the speed rate.

The exhibitors have to supply the pulleys for
the main shafts, as well as any other gear and
driving bands, at their own cost.
Machinery intended to be worked will be
placed in the central gallery of the machinery

The rreservation, cleaning, and oiling of the
main shafts will be attended to by the Austrian
General Manager, but exhibitors will have to
attend to the preservation and oiling of the gear
supplied by them, as also to the security of their
straps.
Brickwork foundations in the machinery hall
must be built at:the cost
.of the exhibitors, and be
finished and ready for receiving the machinery
by the 16th of March, 1873; but the brick founda-
tions and the stonework for engines and steam-
boilers, &c., employed for setting in motion the
machines exhibited, will he constructed by the
Austrian Commission according to the plans of the
exhibitors. •

The main lines of pipes far water, steam, and
gas will also be laid by the Austrian Commission,
and the exhibitor has only to supply the connect-
ing pipes with his machines.

Coals from the beat Austrian and Prussian coal
mines, and feeding water for boilers, Sze., sup-
plying steam• engines, driving {machinery in the
machinery hall, will be supplied by the Austrian
Commission free of expense. Stokers will also be
provided for the steam boilers lent for service in
the Exhibition, or, if the exhibit(); shouli prefer
to employ his own people, the wages of the latter

ALM, 1±

will be paid by tlid Austrian Commission according

to the fixed tariff.

Should an:exhibitor wish to burn wool, he will
likewise be provided with it.
The whole Exhibition ground will be drained by
a system of drainage. pipes, carrying Water aud
liquids to the Danube,: and every measure has
been taken to leaie a Sufficient supply of water la
all parts of the Exhibition.
Water will be fuinished at a pressure of about
24fr. at low pressure, and about 120 ft. at high

pressure.
Gas will he farnishea by the Imperial C9ati-
nontal Gas Company at the usual presiure.
Steam pressure generslly at five atmospheres,
about 70 to the square inch.

Steam pressure in foreign boilers is not limited,
but they will be subject to thelAustrian laws and
regulations. .
Single boiler-houses are being erected at the rear
of the machinery hall, about 40ft. distant; but it
special boiler-house for British, boilers will be
built by the Austrian Conimission.
Plans furnished by the Britishrommission far
British boiler -houses will be adopted, if the
British Commission will undertake the execution of
the same. The erection of British boiler-houses
especially desired, in order to show the ingenuity
and workmanship of British construction.
Traction engines, locomotive steam carriages for
ordinary roads, steam omnibuses, and similar
kinds of self-propelling vehicles, will be allowed
to run about during the Exhibition in some parts
of the park and the Exhibition grounds. In fact,
traction engines, road rollers, self-propelling
steam carriages, steam omnibuses, and steam
pleasure carriages will be very welcome.
There will be some work of importance to be
done by steam road rollers, and in case of any
wrrli performed for the installation by traction
engines or road rollers, all expenses will be paid
by the Austrian Commission.
In case of railway locomotive engines and, car-
riages being sent to the Exhibition, the rails for
them to stand upon must be provided by tlie ex-
hibitors, and it is very much desired that
,rails from
England should be sent to Vienna as Exhibition
articles.

There will be corapetitive7:trials with steam
fire engines, and the jury and the, exhibitors are
invited to send special engines for this purpose.
Such engines will be considered as objects of ex-
hibition, and if lent for use, fuel and care will be
at the charge of..the Imperial] Austrian Commis-
sion.

There w,ill likewise be speciall trials
,held with
agricultural machinery and implements in fields in
the neighbourhood of Vienna, or in such places as
can be easily reached by the Exhibition railway.
Agrioultural machines will not be exhibited in
the machinery hall, but in a pavilion specially
built for that purpose.
All machines, &e., intended for the Exhibition
will be admitted to the machinery hall from the
the Ist of February till the 15th of April, 1873,
inclusive, and must.be set up by the 25th of April.
Machines and apparatus arriving in pieces, and
consisting of heavy and bulky parts, must be act
up by the 15th of April.

Slate is particularly desired to be sent to tbo
:Exhibition; the slate will stand a chance of being
sold with advantage at the close of the Exhibi-
tion, the Austrian slate being only fit for roofing.
It is also desired by the Director-General that
fittings, show-cases, cloth for the covering of
walls, window glass, &c., should -be sent frail
England to Vienna; these would be consid.erea
Exhibition object; and could be sold at the oluse
of the Exhibition.

Considering the bad and very costly experiences
of all foreign commissions at past London and
Paris Exhibitions in storing empty packing cnseg'
the Director-General of the Austrian Commission'
has made special arrangements in this respeot
offering every possible facility. He has secured
near, the Exhibition grounds a large space for
"empties," which he offers gratis to the foreign
,commissions. On this space a modern building
will be erected, and a very moderate ntte charged
according to a fixed tariff based upon the actual
outlay of cost. It will be connected by rail Nal
the Exhibition buildingi, so that all empties e'sn
be sent direct to this shed.
No previous Exhibition has afforded such
facilities for this purpose.
All applications for information, space, &c., are
to be addressed to Philip Canliffo Owen, rsq'
Secretary to the Royal British Commission for the
Vienna Universal Exhibition; 41, Parliaqient-
street, London, S.W.

The annual reports of the Factory Inspectors
continue to afford a fund of interesting informa-
tion as to the effect of legislative action on the
conditions of labour. Inaidentally we have
much which threws light on the habits and
feelings of the industrial classes. We are
also instructed as to the views entertained by
empleyere, and the prospects of further legis-
lation for the protection of the employed. The
reports are those of Mr. Alexander Redgrave
and Mr. Robert Baker, both extending down
to April 30. The first Factory Act was passed
in 1833, and in August 1871, the administra-
tion of the Workshops Ad was placed under
the superintendence of the inspectors Of
factories.
Among the principal occupations specified.
by Mr. Redgrave as coming under the surveil-
lance of his staff, in virtue of the Workshops
Act, ,are straw nlait schools, straw bonnet
factor*, pillow lace making, hosiery making,
embroidery, hand-loom weaving, artificial
- flower making, cabinet and chair making, hat
and cap making, hoot and shoe making, brick-
making, dressmaking, millinery, tailoring, and
shirt and collar making.. In the districts to
which these and certain other occupations give
a character, wsi are told _ that "thorough
inspection has been made." Children have, heen
sent to school, overcrowding has been remedied,
and the b'aturday half-holiday has been made
a reality. Some opposition has been shown in
the rural districts, but at the same time
• "great forbearance has been exercised towards
the ignorant people who believe their Occupa.
tiona to be unfairly interfered with." With
people of this class Mr. Redgrave has found
the sub-inspectors to have great influence,
"by judiciously and calmly insisting upon
the negessity
,of obserying the law." Upon
the Whole, 'employers are found decidedly
ready to accept thin regulations, and parents
i
are becoming convinced that the law s bene-
The change for the better which is going
on through the mass of the nation is apparent
in the increased readiness with Which legisla-
tion like that. of the Factory and Workshops
Act is complied with. The. Workshops Act
is a remarkable test of the reality and depth
of this improvement. Mr. Redgrave says that
"to those who remember the hickerings of
manufacturers and inspectors under the old
Fedora, Acts; the wholesale complaints of the
inspectors, and the Sledges of the manufac-
turerssto evade the law, it is little Jess than
marvellous to note the cordial co-operation of
the masters of these .workshops,' their readiS
ness to accept our suggestions, and their
anxiety
,to observb the slaw." In examining
the tepees of the Sub-inspectors week by
week, recording visits to hundreds of work-
shops of all kinds and classes, and in every
variety of locality, ,Mr. Redgrave says he'finds
but few infriogernents of the reguletione. The
extent te which the law now operates is well
expresand by Mr. Redgrave when he Says that
the ad of• 1867 "embraced in its almost
universal provisions a blast furnace, a brick-
field, and a London dressmaker's work-room."
Mr. Baker writes somewhat differently from
Mr. Redgrave, though in the main his conclu-
siions are the same. Speaking of the Work-
shops . Act, ha says—" We visit. places now
situated in the courts and alleys of large
towns, into which the sun can scarcely ever
enter, to.elamthe heats Of 'old cottages already
worn out with long service, now converted
into factories, and worked by the dwindled
power of small high-pressure engines, crowded
with occupants oblivious, of the pride of plaoe,
and caring little for those appliances which in
theniselves constitute the reasons for sanitary
investigations."
TI% oocial aspect of the people impresses
naliei rather gainfully. He,eays----" We
marvel to see women at the anvil and forge,
and men nursing while the wives toil for the
week& Wags; and infants everywhere mew-
ling in the arms of other infants very little
older . than theinselyee, till ono begins to
think that the old, old days of factory labour
have returned, and wonder whether what Wa
see ears possibly exist in the advanced period
of 1872.•
"
We take- these ataternents as proof that the
iiaw which regulatee labour is 11UW descending
pato a lower stratum, where its beneficent
bparation is greatly needed, and *hero, as Mr.
Baker presently says, 'there isst vast field for
- philanthropic effort."
The Nina tfatus 13111 of the present session
s dieoassed by Mr. Redgrave, who argues that
tlie nine-hour sylitem Of the engineering trade
is a very different thing from that which is
• proposed by thiiebilis Ilesays, "lam informed
that over-tins° is constantly worked in all the
trades in which overtime has been used recently
to as great, if; not to a greater, -extent thau
ever it had been before:" He states that he
had an instance given him a short time since
•Sir a martufeeturing engineer who had conceded
• the nine-hour system, and. during the week
, preceding his (Mr. Redgrave's) inquiry the
men in the • service • of this employer had
worked 84:hours, -receiving pay for 105 fhours.
• Mr. Redgrave eonaeonently. argues that "the
• real nine-hour intsvement,.' commencing at
liewcastle7ein-Tyne, was-not founded, like the
Factory Acts, upon the ground that the hour

Of work were oppressively, long, and ought tp
be shortened, but originated in the desire of
the operatives for a fresh basis for the settle-
ment of wages. Perhaps the present agita-
tion.anaong the building trades is of the same
character. At all events, Mr. Itedgrave holds
that the .Nine Hours Bill for the textile trades
,is not on all fours with the nine-hour system
of the mechanics.

The argument that the augmented. speed of
machinery is throwing an increased strain on .
the operatives in the textile manufactures is
placed by Mr. Redgrave in juxtaposition with
the statement of the masters that machinery
has been so improved as to relieve and benetit
the employed: .Mr. Redgrave observes, "It
is not easy to strike a balance between these
Statements, both made on the most trust-
worthy authority." It is remarkable that in.
some instances the hours of work in factories
have been reduced to 5p and. 55 hours per
week by voluntary arrangement. Among the
former are the 11. ax and jilt() factories of
Dundee, and the silk works of Derby and
Nottingham. Netwithstanding the good that
has been 'aCconiiilished,, and is still going
on, 'Mr. Redgrave says :—"There are Many
thing's in the Factory Act
.which require'
alteration," and which the present proposed
legislation would not touch; although the evils
" really cry aloud for: amelioration." Child.
labour is still too freely. employed. . Children
begin toil too early in life, and may. in many:
eases be legally worked. too long. On the
question of female . employment Mr.. Baker
dwells at length, and greatly deplores the
.extent to which young married women addict
themselves to a factory life, to the neglect of
their honiest and the injury of their children..
Mr. Reclgrave,, in reference to this part of the
subjoet, says, "This question.inust wait for the
education of the men,theinselye' and we fear
that is the only solution or pretty nearly so.

On Saturday the first of a series of fetes, to

THE PORTLAND BREAKWATER.

The prince of Wales opened this great work
on Saturday, and a few figures and .measure-
ments will give some idea of this large under-
taking, which, now that it is finished, offers
to the eye. little more than a thin reef,
stretching Away aimed till it fades. This
great sea-wall stretches with a bend towards
Weymouth for a mile and live-eighths from the
east aide of the island of Portland, and shelters
from every wind an area of 2,100. acres Of
water, 1,290 of which have at low tides a
depth ranging from five to 11 fathoms. It
consists of an inner breakwater, 1,900 feet in
length, divided from an outer or isolated break-
water, 6,200 feet in length, by an Opening 400
feet wide. The whole is built in nine to ten
fathoms of water, the material nsed being
rough blocks of Portland stone, quarried by
convicts from the shore close by. This was
loaded into trucks, which were ran out on a'
scaffolding and tipped into tlie sea, the scaf-
folding being pushed forward as the reef of
rooks rose above the-Water. The inner break-
water, has. been built with dressed stone into a
finished sea-wall, the surface of which is two
broad roadways, the outer raised above the
inner on arched recesses for the reception of
Government stores. Its magnitude and
strength are buried for ever out of sight, and
we have to remember that if the Botta could
run dry that low line of stime Would grow to
a vast Cyclopean wall, 100 ft. high, and 100
yards thick- at the base. It is -heaped up by,
nearly six million tons of stone, which, if built
-into a solid column 100 ft. in diameter, would
overtop the highest Alp. Another, and indeed
the chief, marvel and difficulty of the under-
taking was the erection of the scaffolding, of
which, of course, there now remains no trace.
It- must be deseribed as a wooden railway
viaduct of .the most massive kind, built a Mile
and a half out from the shore, in from 36ft.. to
60ft of. rough , sea„ Water. Every timber had
to be made waterproof and wormproof by the
hydraulic forcing Of creosote into the pores of
the weed, and when this was done a huge pile
was made of nine or tentimbers bolted together
in one mighty' spar of eight or nine tons, some
two or three feet square. Tipped with an
iron sarew, this was lowered into the sea till
it rested on the bottom, when it was worked
round by a capstan till the screw had bitten
Bft.. into the clay. Three or four of these
great piles: *ere sot at a time, and at once
bolted together by many wrought-iron tie-rods
and powerful cross timbers and under trusses
till the mass was strong enough to carry the
trucks of stone for "tipping in." The top of
the scaffolding was 301 t. above the water, or
901 t. above the ground. In the construction
of the North Fort these piles were set in two
great circles of 112 ft. and 2241 t. in diameter,
upon which, LIS on a huge 'dial, moved an
immense wrought-iron \ radial "traveller,"
dragging the feeding trains, each with from
60 to 80 bons Of Stone in tow, stopping them
over the exaot.spot where more "tipping" was
required, when, as by magic, the waggons
rose on end, and poured their blocks into the
seourged and lettered waves. Thus—and,
this snows the way in which the whole break-
water was built—a mighty mound was heaped
for the foundations of the North Fort, an
island in the sea,: of 140,000 tons of solid stone,
and, with the fortifications, 100 ft. high, 400 ft.
'in diameter at the base, and 200 ft. at the
summit. The total cost of the breakwater
and harbour works, including the coaling
eitablishment, jetties, and waterworks, has
been £1,033,600,. a sum which represents
Money paid out of the nation's pocket to
contractors and others, and has nothing what-
ever to do with the worth of the

labour.

and then there is a new birth, a painful

struggle, and a happy release, and so the
foolish game goes on "world without end."
It would only tend to irritate the projectors
and friends of these literary abortions were
wo to call them over by their proper titles.
But does it not seem strange that there should
be an Anti-Game Law paper, a Working
Man's Anti-War paper, a Railway Employ6s'
_ _

paper, an Ironworkers' paper, an Agricultural
Labourers' paper, a Bakers' paper, and many
others of a like kind "too tedious to men-
tion." It is presumed that these sheets serve
the causes they are set on foot to represent,
and perhaps in a slight way they do.
But do the resources thus absorbed pro-
duce as good a result as they might if
otherwise employed. A continued representa-
tion of the same ideas to the same people is not
wholesome. It too frequently narrows men's
views, and produces the weakness of bigotry
rather than the strength which grows out of
more general studies ; and at best it confines
sometimes what would be useful as general
Information, to a limited audience. There is
not one of these special papers which does not
contain matter interesting and useful to the
general public, but shut in thus, only those
who least need it have the opportunity of
seeing it.

It can scarcely be wondered at that, whilst
Buell a system of teaching prevails, the work-
ing men are divided into small sections with
limited and partial views of each other's
requirements and duties ; and indifferent or
antagonistic to each other when the highest
interests demand they should be deeply con-
cerned in eaeh other's proceedings, and
united for the promotion of each other's
welfare.

If they would look at their situation like
sensible men, and above all things try to
understand how their separate interests are
rooted in common principles, their strength
for any good purpose would be tenfold what
it is; whilst their aggressive power, in
advancing against the barriers of prejudice,
self-interest, and oppression, whether by
power in the State, or by capital in its in-
jurious operations in the field of industry,
would be simply irresistible.

We stand now at the commencement of an
epoch which will prove itself to be one of the
most remarkable in the history of the world.
Industry in its usefulness, its dignity, its
beneficence, is asserting itself. The workers
are declaring in favour of principles of right
and justice whieh, to suit them, must be
universally applicable, as what is equit-
able to the masses of the people, cannot be
oppressive or in any way unjust to any
separate section of the community. The
sectional in the now order of things must be
absorbed by the general; and it is, therefore,
gross blunder on the part of working men to
break themselves up into knots and parties
with the view of preaching and cultivating
petty interests instead of urging on public
attention that higher and more general thought
—that deeper and truer sense of the public
interest to which our present fragmentary
teaching renders us lamentably behind. No
general strength comes out of any number of
separate weaknesses; but, by the combination
of these,we may utilize what is in them of power
for the promotion of the public good. Iron-
workers, bakers, and. agricultural labourers,
railway men, and others, instead of each
seeking to keep a weak journal afloat, should
try if, by their combined efforts, they cannot
give life and. power to one strong journal,
which shall explain the principles in which
they all are interested, record. the action in
which they are all engaged, outline the policy
profitable for all to adopt, and, thus give to the
whole labour movement a force and meaning
it never can possess whilst broken, divided,
and groping in a kind, of confusing twilight
after leaders, many of whom are themselves
perplexed and bewildered as to the course they
should pursue.
We attribute no discreditable personal
motives; we believe all this fragmentary work
may be done, and. is done, very honestly;
or do we care for any injurious suspicion
levelled at ourselves—such a thing may be re-
garded as a matter of course. Still we are
satisfied, that the interests of labeur call for

the policy we recommend; and. when our
working men are wise enough to adopt and
carry it out with spirit, the cause of
labour will at once become a question of the
highest national importance, and its emanci-
pation will only be delayed by lack of neces-
sary knowledge to carry forward the great
work in a fitting manner.

THE ARMY AND THE AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.
IN. the Daily News of Monday, a letter
appeared from an agricultural labourer, calling
attention to the fact in very ungrammatical,
but highly significant language, that soldiers
had appeared in the harvest-field to aid the
farmers against the discontented labourers,
and, as a matter of the sheerest necessity,
compel the poor labourer to put up with his
wretched starvation allowance of wages. The
Daily News treats the proceeding, as a matter
of course, as the ordinary leave given to
soldiers to go into the market and sell their
labour. It may or may not be this, we believe,
with their labouring-man correspondent, that
such is not the case. As we noticed this
matter a fortnight since, in consequence of a
paragraph which then appeared, to the effect
that certain farmers had waited on the military
authorities at Aldershot, with the view of
arranging for the employment of soldiers'
labour in getting in the harvest. We have this
antecedent fact, therefore, to go upon, and we
have the subsequent fact mentioned in the
farm labourer's letter to give it meaning, that
in the locality where he resides the soldiers
are displacing the labourers, and, as he states,
taking their children's bread out of their mouths.
Taking this matter, therefore, as it is placed
before us, we regard it not only as a great
wrong to the labourers, but as a dangerous
incitement to breaches of the peace. Perhaps
our military authorities think a little blood-
letting at the present time would do good.
Possibly they would like to vary their Autumn
Mancouvres by hunting and shooting down
discontented labourers, and thus adding a little
real blood to the sham fighting now going on
as a.matter of histrionic effect. We beg, how-
ever, to tell the authorities, civil and
military, as well as those who are otherwise ,
interested in the matter, as farmers and land-
lords, that they are playing a dangerous
game; and that if they proceed in it they will
arouse the angry hostility of every man in the
country who earns the bread of his children
by the labour of his hands. This is not a
political question upon which men may differ,
and for the settlement of which they can
afford to wait. It is in fact, and in truth, a
question of life and death, in which it would
be the merest folly to counsel patience and
forbearance to those immediately and most
directly injured. Mr. CARDWELL talks of
teaching trades to soldiers, such as the build-
ing and other trades, and his arrangements
for this purpose have already been partly
made. 'We tell him now that unless the
soldiers are at once drawn out of competition
with the agricultural labourers, he will never
be permitted by the working men of England
to carry out his new scheme. -Whatever else
they may be prepared for, they are not pre-
pared to allow the Government to train the
army as competitors with themselves in the
labour market; and if the present Government
was not struok with political fatuity, they
might have seen this. How can they look for
the support of working men at the next
general election whilst open to a charge like
his?

But in the meantime is the peace of
the nation safe in the presence of such a
fact? Let it not be forgotten by any
one of our comfortable classes, by any
one of our rulers—civil or military—that
wois have in England, in our big towns
and in our fields, masses of people who
have never been cared for or educated in
any Sway into thought, and, therefore, into
patience, who are not partakers in our civiliza-
tion, and who have no means but their labour,
day by day, to supply their most pressing
wants. These people, unhappily, at the pre-
sent moment, are suffering sorely by the high
price of food. Already we hear of excited
gatherings and turbulent mobs; the smoke is
alarmingly visible, the flame may at any

moment shoot up and send its lurid glare
throughout the land. What begins in bread
riots, or rows between soldiers and farm
labourers, may end nobody knows where, or
in what. We implore the Government,
therefore, to be wise in time, to draw back in
this matter whilst they have the power, before
they are compelled to ruthlessly suppress riot,
or make a shameful compromise with disorder
and tumult. There is yet time to prevent
calamities every good citizen would deplore,
and that time should not be allowed to slip
by unimproved. The competition of the army
with working men in the ordinary fields of in-
dustry must inevitably lead to a cruel war of
class against class. Let the Government be-
ware lest by their folly, prejudice, or blind-
ness they excite this. We say it again, and
we do so most emphatically, that if they
persevere in this, their supporters will be
swept at the next election from every hustings
in England where working men can make
effective the electoral power they possess.

articles.title: PROPOSED PEOPLE'S PALACE AND PARK..
articles.text:
THE PROPOSED PEOPLE'S PALACE
AND PARK..

ALTHOUGH the promising scheme for making
the Alexandra Palace and Park an easy and
efficient means of popular recreation and in-
struction on the principle of Tontine came to
nothing, Mr. FULLER, the projector, has
revised his plan under the form of a public
company with limited liability and under
auspices which givelgoodihopelof success and
general gratification. The LORD MAYOR has
readily consented to place himself in his
official capacity at the head of a strong com-
mittee pledged to carry out the design. The
value of this body of gentlemen consists less in
the influential character of the individual
persons, though numbering men who join to
high rank and station a true nobility of charac-
ter and a sincere desire to promote the welfare
and happiness of the whole community, than
in the fad that it embraces representative
men of every grade in society, ani exerting
every kind of good influence. The avowed pur-
pose of the company being to make the palace
and park, not simply a means of easy, cheap,
and, instructive recreation, but in very deed
the property of the peolo, to the extent, at
least, to which the people may think proper
to take shares, our confidence in the scheme
and in its success is increased and confirmed
by observing on the committee the names of
men who have proved their earnest and intel-
ligent interest in the happiness of the working
classes, and of other men who themselves are
members of those classes. No better guarantee
of the sort could be afforded than the presence
in the same committee of such representatives
of the people as Lord LICHFIELD, Alderman
LUSK, Mr. SAMUEL MORLEY, Mr. THOMAS
BRASSEY, Sir .Tourr BErrifErr, Mr. CHARLES
REED, and Mr. M'CULLAGU TORRENS, and
several leading men of the people.

The sub-committee of five well-chosen gen-
tlemen having reported as to the terms and
conditions on which the owners are prepared
to make a transfer of the property, the General
Committee will prove itself admirably well
calculated, by the large diversity of views
and interests with respect to other matters
which it represents in its composition, to carry
out the declared objects in the most satisfac-
tory and unexceptionable manner. Mr.
FULLEII believes himself to have demonstrated
the substantial nature of the financial basis
on which his project rests; and, so far as we
can see, there is nothing fallacious or unre-
liable in his anticipations. The success of
the experiment depends upon promptitude,
unanimity, and. general co-operation. Ile pro-
poses to divide the capital in shares of one
pound each. As a matter of course, the
holders of shares will have tickets of admission
to the palace and grounds on the easiest terms.
As to dividends upon shares, the holders will
have the option of taking them in money, or
in Art Union tickets. The prizes will vary
in value from not less than two pounds to as
much as five hundred pounds each. Thus the
lowest prize will be twice the money invested,
and the distribution of prizes will be yearly.
The drawers of prize-tickets will be entitled
to select what they have won from an exhibi-
tion in the Palace of articles marked with
their respective values. A. great variety is
intended, in order to meet all testae and all

desires, but without losing sight of those com-
binations of pleasure with utility in which art
workmanship is a prominent feature, and
which are therefore adapted to elevate and
improve the perceptions of industrial minds,
and to minister at once to their social delight
and family convenience.

The extensive use made of the parks by
the people in the neighbourhood of large
towns sufficiently proves the high value
set upon such accommodation, and the im-
proved moral influence set in motion as a con-
sequence. Perhaps, however, the restrictions
imposed by the superintending authorities are
somewhat too many and severe for thorough
and free enjoyment. The working classes
will have a fuller sense of liberty when they
find themselves ranging at will over a domain
entirely and absolutely their own. Every day
will have its separate attractions; but special
provision will be made for the time-honoured
observance of "Saint Monday" and annual
or occasional holidays. As one result of the
proposed arrangements, it is hoped that the
reputed patron saint of the British workman
will be less honoured, and less exclusively, by
libations of malt liquors than in former times,
through the substitution for the tap-room and
the ale-bench of other attractions more rational
in themselves, and more conducive to rationality
in all respects. For a single sixpence in-
dividuals will be able to go there and back,
and see all that is to be seen, and, enjoy
all that is to be enjoyed. Provision will
be made for the conveyance and admission
of societies, clubs, schools, and other com-
panies of old and young. Outdoor amuse-
ments of every kind will be added to the
indoor pleasures of the Palace. Mothers will
be enabled to refresh their children with milk
and butter produced upon the spot, and parties
of all ages will have ample means of ()heap and
wholesome refreshment as well as of innocent
and instructive recreation. We honestly feel
that, after the simple statement of these facts
and provisions, it would be superflous to
employ either argument or persuasion to
incline our readers for taking as many shares
in the concern as their means and eiromn.
stances will justify.

•TO.M. FOOLERY.

WE do not take it as part of our duty as
journalists to preach sermons to working men
on their sins and shortcomings. There are
so many who take a pleasure in this, and who,
therefore, pursue the practice so actively, that
without our help we are sure all that can be
done is accomplished as correction by reproof.
Besides, after all, the sins which ask for most
frequent censure amongst working men are
those also most observable in other classes of
the community. Sensible men laugh at the
frippery of courts, whether seen in Europe,
accompanied by the refinement of civilized
life, or in Africa amongst the greasy savages,
who travestio them with a becoming sense of
their utility in supporting kingly power. In
England working men are presumed to be
capable of seeing through such tawdry
nonsense, and fine speeches are addressed to
them on the supposition that such is the case.
After all, however, we must recognize things
as they are, and if we are sensible men we
must accept the truest tests possible for dis-
covering the moral and intellectual tendencies
of our people—if by writing or speech we
desire to exercise any effective influence on the
men with whom we have to deal. It is all
very well for a few persons to get together in
a corner, give themselves some compre-
hensive title,
.and address themselves to the
working people as intelligent strugglers, seek-
ing to bring about that indefinite but happy
condition of things prefigured under the title
of "the good time coming." But if any
practical man desires to fix the date of this
much desired time by finding out how much
of earnestness and geed sense there is in the
working people, be should plant himself on the
south side of London Bridge, andobserve care-
fully what tnkesplace when some great working
Some of the orders are modest enough,
man's fete is about to to held at the Crystal
regards costume, scarves and extraordinary
Istisltaalrraesegbeae.ing the only conspicuous ornaments, and
these, we presume, are confined to office
bearers. They are, however, sufficiently
tawdry in appearance to create the suspicion

10

that they are the cast-off ornaments of
some improving tribe of savages who had
become ashamed of them.

The great triumph in this sort of thing,
however, belongs to the Foresters, putting
aside scarves, stars, and. all else, their remark-
able ROBIN HOOD dresses are of themselves
sufficient to strike all beholders with wonder.
A grand day at court where orders are dis-
played, and where all the glitter and show
are real, has very little to relieve it from the
rklioulous ; but these sham displays, all tinsel
and tawdry, almost necessarily provoke
laughter. The Odd-Fellows triumph by high
sounding titles. Their "noble gra.nds" and
other "grand's" almost take people's breath away
until thy becomeused to them. They are harm-
less, nodouht, as displays of folly, unless, indeed,
there is harm, which we more than suspect,
in an apeing of titles and trumpery which
almost goes to prove an innate ineradicable
love in men for, frippery and folly, and that
from a fish bone in the cartilage of the nose to
the collar of the Knights of the Garter we
have a sign of weakness common to every
creature brought . into the. world by the
daughters of EVE. We are perfectly aware
that all these societies do noble work by the
feeling of brotherhood they cultivate, and the
relief they administer. But why, we ask,
should , they be so extravagant in a tore
foolery which partially turns into grotesque-
ness what is.in itself so useful through the
good it aceomplishes, and so touehin'g by the
fraternal affection, out of whieh it takes its
rise. If the same work could be done without
the attendant folly, a.great point would be
gained, not on the side of commonsense alone,
but also on that of political progress. To be
weaned from such infantile tastes would
itself be an indication of a truer manliness in
life than we can hope for whilst our working
men continue to treasure the rags and tinsel of
an old fraudulent superstition.

articles.title: MB,. MOON ON MIXES.
articles.text:
MB,. MOON ON MIXES.

WE may guess at the actual thought of Par-
liament by listening to the utterances of men
out of it, belonging to the classes who chiefly
people the benches of the House of Commons.
Those inside are more careful. They know
they speak With the "eyes of the world"
upon them, or at least with the eyes of certain
working men constituents watching them,
and in eonseduence of this they moderate the
class folly and prejudice by which so many of
them are animated. At county gatherings,
meetings of railway shareholders, and other 1
such assemblages, they address themselves to
respectable people in a sort of confidential and
unconstrained way, and speak of the working
people and thou r proceedings with a freedom
Which lets us completely into their confidence,
,
as apostles of political truth and upholders of
middle and tipper class interest.
Air. Roman Meorr the other day, at the
luilf-yearly meeting ef the 'Auden and North-
Western .liailway, . shareholders, _furnished a
strong instance of this frankness. As chairman
of that assembly, Kr. geol. had to refer to
the great advance in the Price of coals, and
whilst doing this his discursive fancy led him
off into other .pu,bjeots relative,to the present
exceptional state of things ia oonne' (Alen with
the working of our railway?. Of course he had
eomething to Hey about the interfcrenee of
outsiders.", Naturally enough Mr. MOON
objects to‘. these, though outsidere will, no
doubt, continue to intermeddle with railway
management; at.least, Po long as their lives
and limbs are at the mercy_of " insiders," and
so long as the risks of accidents. to these are
increased by the bad
,treatment, of the men
employed by the companies.. But the most
curious portion of his 00Mments. sheuld
be stated in his own woYds. "He must
say that the interference of outsiders ' who
misled the men was deplorable. The other
day he was shooked, to see that the iron and
steel, which were now in use in their works at
Crewe, were foreign. These strikes had
opened up new sources of supply and of uolnlie-
Wien, which otherwise might have reinained
long unexplored, but which, once opene&-
would. never, again. be Owed." This .oarious
statement was followed by a _hearty sympa-
thetic, "hear, hear," which no doubt expressed
as fully as a dozen columns of indignant

speech could, the disapproval of the assemblei
shareholders.

Dear iron and steel; it seems, have brought
foreign iron and steel into our markets, and
the high price of the horae-made articles thus
driven out is due to strikes. Can anything be
clearer than this, and should not every man
who wishes well to the commerce of the
country set ,his face sharply against the
trades unions by which we are so frequently
dragged into these strikes? We do not know
what Mr. MOON is; he may be an iron and
steel maker, or he may have large estates in
the Isle of sky. Whatever he is ,he should
knovvotnething about the matter upon which
be addressed his audience. Taking his words
as they stand, he must be either very ignorant
or slightly reticent, or he could not possibly.
have uttered them. Without any inquiry on
special points necessary to be understood in
this matter, and without any knowledge
whatever of the special ease adduced, we do
not hesitate. to say that Mr. MOON'S state-
ment in its plain meaning, as spoken to his
shareholders and as published in the papers, is
not true, and cannot be correct. He ought to
have stated whether the iron was Swedish,,
and, if so, whether it was imported because of
its cheapness, or because of some special fit-
ness for the work in Which it Was einployed.
Again, he mighthave said how the surplus above
the average price of iron was disposed of.
Into whose pockets it went, aud in what pro-
portions. If irOn. is £8 a ton above the natural
cost Of production, does the maker and merchan t
-get it, or does it go to enrich the workers ?
ltr. Moo* knows, or ought ,to know, that

for one penny the men get the maker and
merchant get a shilling. The price of the
.commodity is put up by these gentlemen, and
not by the operative. If in the machine and
engineering shops of the country there was no
more serious rise in iron and steel than what
Was rendered necessary by advanced wages,
foreign iron and steel could not be imported
to advantage. Ent, when makers and dealers
in iron and steel add pound after pound to its
price per ton, they give foreigners a chance,
which could not be otherwise opened to them,
of bringing goods into the British markets.
We do not blame them for this. According
to our received economic gospel, they have a
perfect right to do so, whatever effect it may
have on the future industry of the country.
It is not this we grumble at, but we grumble,
and, yo think, justly, when men like Mr.
MOW. 7 deliberately lead the public astray by
blaming strikes for uuduly advancing prices;
when, he knows that whatever blame may
belong to eueli a proceeding rests fairly on the
heads of others.
Let us deal honestly with each other,
Trades unions may be most culpable ,bodies,
but this not the question between us and Mr.
Moo. The question is, who has put up the
price of English iron and steel so as to lead to
the importations complained.of, and. into whofrie
pockets has this unpatriotic gain. gone ? We
challenge Mr. Moor to descend to particulara
in this matter, and, in any view of it, we defy
him to prove his case. We assert that in hia
desire to misrepresent trades unions, he has

been leading the public mind astray, and we
call on him to justify his words, or accept thi,
character they cannot fail to fasten on him if
he makes nuatempt to sustain them by the
evidence of facts.

FARMER'S' friends were at one time a very
numerous party, but at their best they were
few compared to labourert?.frielids at the pre-
sent moment, The old 'farmers' friends were

whilst modern labourers friends think of

comfortable; but then they wish them to be
so Moderate in their demands as to prevent
any interest suffering through their improve-
ment. If they could all ride on high horses

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS'
MOVEMENT.
Mr,. LLEWELLYN DAMS'S admirable paper
published in the Guardian, on " Latxntrers'
Combinations from ti Clerical Point of Piety,"
contains some interesting observations with
regard to the difficulty of applying tho Union
principle to unskilled labour. On this ho
writes as follows :--
- '

How much an agricultural labourers' union may
be able to effect for its members is a question not
easy to answer. The objects of the Warwickshire
Union are thus described :—To raise wages, to
lessen the hours of labour, to promote the improve-
ment of cottages, to obtain allotments, and to
assist the migration of lahourors. The rate of
wages aimed at is ills. a week in 'ordinary times,
and 30s. during harvest. There are difficulties in
the way of these agricultural unions which have
not previeusly been enconntered by trades' unions.
It is a new thing, as I have already said, to form
a union of men whose labour is little better than
unskilled. A. union has hitherto been—l think
invariably—the union of a trade; that is, of men
-who could not be replaced except by others simi-
larly trained and skilled, of men with reasonably
good wages who could pubscribe liberally, and
subsist for a time without ,employnient. To many
trades' unionists, I imagine, it must have seemed
a hopeless attempt to construct a union of farm
labourers. But, besides their extreme Poverty,
and the nearly unskilful character of their labour,
the variations in the seasons must make it difficult
for these labourers in combination to insist on any
specific terms. A vigorous and extensive union
might have the farmers at its mercy during the
height of harvest time; and, on the other hand
in winter the farmers might retaliate with pain-
ful effect, The danger of carrying a contest to
extremity is likely to tell on the men moie than
the einployers. It seems possible, therefore, that
be operations of unions may be comparatively
feeble, and may disappoint those who have hoped
too much from them. But it will hardly be denied
that the movement has decidedly helped that rise
•of wages which has been very general in the
country districts. It is no small matter that men
who had been receiving 12a. a week should have
suddenly found themselves in receipt of los.
I do not pretend to have an opinion as to the
demands which may be made with right and with
hope of success by the labourers in rural districts.
But on two points we need not entertain any
doubt. That migration of labour, with which
the name of Mr. Girdlestone is so honourably
associated, and which is obviously rational and
desirable, is an object which a union may wisely
propose to itself to promote. A union may collect
and diffuse information on this matter' and may
supply the means of travelling, so as to better the
condition both of those who go and of those who
stay. The other point is the substitution of a
money equivalent for the allowanees front the
farmer by which the labourer's wages have been
eked out. That a labouring man should be partly
. paid in bad cider is an altogether notious custom.
tioine of the other allowances are unobjectionable
in themselves, but any payment in kind is now
humiliating, and a source of discontent. A good-
natured farmer will not be prevented from doiny
good-natured things in his dealings with his
men, but it seems to be most desirable that there
should be no longer any understanding as to
allowances being a supplement to wages. An
English working man in these
,days ought to be
able to know, exactly. -what he earns, and to be
able to spend his wages according to his own dis-
cretion. ,
There are certain desirable results, therefore,
which I think we may confidently expect will be
directly brought about by, the combinations of
agricultural labourers.. But. I repeatl that my
main argument for them is that they are sure to
increase the self-respect oncl indepoubno o ote
labourer.

THE WORK AND WAGES OF THE

LONDON POSTMEN.

PART I.—WORK.
Most persons have heard of the simple Irishman
who, having posted a letter, stood for some time
patiently waiting for the answer to jump out of

the box into his hands; and though we laugh at
his simplicity, few of us possess a much clearer

_
idea of the manner in which a letter is made to I
reach its destination after leaving our hands.
Those who think it a very simple matter to for-
ward a missive to a given address, would be
astonished at the multiplicity and complexity of
the arrangements necessary to effect that Even
the few individuals who may have been favoured
with a private view of the internal arrangements
of the Post Office, can hardly have any clear idea
of the system by which the correspondence of this
great commercial
,nation is made to circulate
almost as regularly as the blood within our veins.
The day's work at the General Post Office
begins at 5 a.m., and all who arrive late sign their
names in a boo)c kept for that purpose, and at the
end of each month are called
,upon for a:yritten
explanation, and punished with extra duty, with-
out pay, for their want of punctuality. .

Passing through the yard we see a number of
vans and carts, front which the sacks of letters and
papers that have come from varbus parts of the
country are being secured by porters. These are
carrrod into the offico and shot ont promiscuously
on what are technically called" facing tables,"
whore a number of men are ready to " face "
them.; that is, to place them all with the addresses
the same way, and the stamps to the right-hand
corner. Others, called clearers, take them pp
dexterously in long rows, and place them on other
tables ready for the stampers. This clearing is a
more difficult operation than it appears to be; for
if it happens that a "nobbly " one (that is, a letter
containing anything which will not lie flat) is
placed in or near the centre of the row, the whole
arm.full will slip suddenly from his grasp when
midway between the facing and the stamping
tables; and the poor fellow is inimediately

greeted with the chaffing cry of "Facing!
facing!" as of course they have all to be re-

arranged.

The stamper has a peculiar skill of his own, not
very easy to acquire. The hand stamp, which is
still in use, consists of an engraved block or die of
metal or wood, in some of which the figures are
moveable, so that the date or number or hour can
be changed at pleasure. This is. fixnd to a short
handle of wood, terminating in a knob; is held
by the two middle and the little finger pressing it
against the lower part of the hand, the fore-finger
and the thumb being perfectly free. It is used in
conjunction with a pad, consisting of several

thicknesses of cloth which is saturated with red
or black paint, and placed inn kind of metal
saucer. The stamp being struck upon this pad,
takei up a portion of paint, which it of course
transfers to the letter when applied to it, leaving
an impression of the device engraved the same as
in printing. If the pad is too wet (that is too
freely supplied with paint), an ugly smudge will,
be the result, whilst if too dry no impression will
be left.

Stamps are of various sorts. There is the
Double, which, at one blow, effaces the Queen's
head, and thus prevents it being again used, and
prints by its side the date of the mouth and the
hour of the day; the Red single, usually placed
upon the back of letters received train the country,
the heads of which have been obliterated at the
office where they were posted; the More to Pay
placed upon letters insufficiently prepaid; and
the Official Paid, placed upon Government com-
municationa, whether upon Postal, War, Treasury,
Customs, or other business, atul which, of course,
are delivered free.

The objects of thus stamping the letters is to
afford means of tracing them through the Office,
so that if complaint is made of delay or mis-
delivery, the party in fault may be discovered.
Various attempts have from time to time been
made to do this stamping by machinery, but none
have been entirely successful; and at the present
time, although there are some machines in use,
a groat part of the work is done by hand. The
stamper is required to keep a register of the
number of the letters passing through his hands,
and for this purpose he is provided with a slip of
paper, upon which ho makes one impression of his
stamp for every hundred, which he afterwards
adds up and signs; a separate tally being kept for
each mail, The average speed is sixty or eighty
per minute, though one hundred and forty have
been done. It is from these tallies that the Official
Returns are made of the number of letters passing
through the Post Office.

On Sunday morning there was a meeting
on Clerkenwell-green to consider the cause
had remedy of the present famine price of
provisions. The meeting was convened under
the auspices of the London Patriotic Society,
and was presided over by Mr. Pottle. The
chairman, in opening the proceedings, referred
to the famine prices which most provisions
fetched at the present time, and said that
working people could not now afford a joint
of meat once a week. He strongly condemned
the working of the Contagious. Diseases
(Animals) Ad, which, he said, was passed as a
system of protection in the interest of home
breeders. The Government should be applied
to on the subject.
Mr. ltiddei then moved, and Mr. Mullins
seconded, the followiug resolution :
" That this meeting protests against the
present working of the Contagious Diseases
(Animals) Acts, in reference to the reStrietions
on .the importation of foreign cattle, as they
are certain that such prohibitions are not used
at present to prevent disease, but to establish
a system of protection in the interest of. home
breeders—a system which, in a nation pledged
to free trade, ought no longer to be tolerated."
This was carried. Mr. Wade then moved,
"That in the opinion of this meeting the land
and game laws are two of the principal causes
of the present dearth of provisions, and pledge
themselves to assist all movements tending

to their abolition."
Mr. Osborne, in seconding the resolution,
drew a comparison between the present and
past prices of provisions, and. defended the
character of Australian meat. The most ex-
traordinary rise had ocourred in that portion
of mutton which was mostly used. by the
working classes—viz., the breast of mutton.
Up to .about six years ago breasts of mutton
were sold at 3th per lb.; the price was now Bd.
per lb. Legs of beef—a most useful part of
the beast to the poor—used to be. sold at 21d.
per lb.; that price had advanced, to 7d. In
their younger days they could get good, sound,
sweet salt . Cork butter-v-as good as need. be
used—for Bd..per,lb., bat now for any butter
they could eat they niust pay Is. 4d. per lb.
On eggs there had eman advance of 60 per
cent., and on lard,bf, 50 per cent.. Coal had
risen something like from 10s. to lls, a ton;
•that was set down to the strikes, but the
miners had. only obtained an increase of is.
per ton itt pay, whilst the rich mine owners
were getting the balance. The practical
question was what was the remedy for all this?
The only immediate one he saw was for work-
men's wives to learn to cook, an art in which
they were exeeedingly deficient. They could
undoubtedly reduce the price of meat by
abstaining from it. As to Australian meat,
in spite of the prejudice existing against it,
it was notorious that every ton of it coming
into England. was bought up by the great
men and distributed over England. If the
prejudice were removed, many millions of
tons of it would. come into this country.
German sausage could not be compared with
good Australian beef or mutton. Lucifer
matches and bundles of wood had advanced
in price, and. penny saveloys had been sub-
jected to a remarkable reduction in size.
The publicans who still sold their beer at 3d.
a quart appeared to be their only friends.
The remedies he proposed, therefore, were—
first, for the people to eat less meat, and,
secondly, to get their wives to try the
Australian "tin" meat. The resolution was
carried.

A.D. 630, Vynegils, King of Wessex, was
there baptised, Oswold, King of Northumbria,
coming to Stand as his sponsor. Thu tee was
removed to Lincoln, A.D. 1100, When ROllllOlB
