articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

A. telegram from Montreal to the New York
papers, received by the Cuba, states that the
Elpanish Vice-Consul has discovered a wide-
spread organization for the enlistment of Vo-
lunteers for the revolutionary army in Cuba in
the principal cities of the Dominion, and con-
centrating them near the Bay of Fundy,
next month, whence they would have been
transferred to a Cuban cruiser. A considerable
number of recruits had been obtained before
the discovery was made.

Quebec, at the departure of the American
mail brought by the Cuba, continued to be
seriously disturbed, owing to the antagonism
between the French Canadians and the Irish.
On one occasion the French made a demon-
stration at St. Roche, and expressed their
determination to attack the Irish head-
quarters. The differences arose out of the
prevention by the Irish of the French ship
labourers working on their wharves. The
Irish made preparations for defence, sonic
field-pieces being placed in position, and at
least a thousand men being drawn up behind
them, armed with rifles and revolvers. No
attack was, however, eventually made. The
respective parties are going about armed, BO
that a collision may occur.

During the passage of the South-Western
Railway Company's steamer the Wonder,
from St. Male to jersey, on Sunday morning,
the vessel became disabled, owing to her air
pump being damaged, when about sixteen
miles off the French coast. A fishing-boat
carried the intelligence of the disaster back to
St. Male, and another steamer was at once
despatched to her assistance. After a long
delay the Wonder was eventually towed into
Large Roads, and the passengers disembarked,
have been on board eighteen hours instead
of the three hours in which the journey is
usually accomplished.

In anticipation of a fresh Carlist raid,
which was planned for Sunday, the Spanish
authorities have asked the French Government
to take repressive measures on the frontier.
Ministerialists indulge in a hopeful forecast
of the elections. They not ouly reckon on a
majority, but on a small and. much-divided
Opposition. The Carlists will abstain, as
before, from voting, and the Sagastinos will,
it is expected, turn out a fractional party.
This good augury is countenanced by the
quiet manner in which the elections have
commenced.

Papal feeling is modifying in Rome. Four
clerical schools have been re-opened, on the
undertaking of their directors to submit to the
laws of the State. Even a bishop has made
his submission, and received the Royal
exequatur.

The Italian Court doctors, Rossi and Bruno,
have left for Ostend to attend upon the Crown
Princess of Italy, who is lying rather danger-
°tidy ill at that town.

j. B. Johnson's gallant attempt to swim
across the Channel has not succeeded. When
he had accomplished seven miles in little more
than an hour his legs grew numb, and, acting
under medical advice, he left the water.
Otherwise he showed no signs of fatigue.

Clerkenwell-green on Sunday witnessed a
creditably regular sad orderly popular assem-
blage, to protest against the high price of
meat, and to pass resolutions condemning the
restrictions on the importation of cattle from
abroad, and. denouncing the Game Laws and
Land. Laws as "two of the principal causes of
the present dearth of provisions.' One of the
speakers strongly urged the expediency of
reclaiming the waste lands of the country,
which would support enough of cattle to feed
the population without recourse to foreign
supplies; and another orator advocated the
taking away of the land from the few holders
of it, on the principle applied by Mr. Gladstone
to the Irish Church—that when a corporate
body did. not apply the property under its con-
trol to proper uses, the State should. step in
and secure the right direction of the funds.

Late on Friday night the Prince of Wales
closed his visit to Trouville, and on Saturday
afternoon the Royal yacht put in at Dieppe,
where it was received without any public
demonstration.

Most unpleasant discoveties have been an-
nounced as to the military equipment of France
during the late war. Absolutely nothing re-
mained in the national arsenals except some
nondescript materiel belonging to the Army
of the Loire, Such is the official report of a
commission of inquiry.

A charaoteristioally patriotic demonstration
has taken place in the theatre at Havre, where
the Republioan Guard gave a concert on
behalf of the orphans in Alsace and Lorraine.
Young Alsatiennos, wearing the national
colours shaded with crape, acted as collec-
tors.

Ratification has been given by the Federal
Counoil of Switzerland to M. Favre's contract
for the construction of the Great St. Gothard
Tunnel.

Prince Milan's majority and accession td
the Government of Servia are being grandly,
celebrated. His people are sending him mag-
nificent presents, and he in turn is giving
magnificent dinners, while the municipality
of Belgrade distinguishes itself by its balls.

Montreal has taken a bad beating from the
English Eleven. In the first innings the
scores were 48 for the Canadian team, and
253 for the English.

An amnesty is the latest incident in Mexican
revolutions. It is said to have been accepted
by most of the insurrectionary leaders, and
another interval of negative peace is hoped
for.

At Liverpool, a sexagenarian hotel-keeper
has been amerced in ,E3OO for breaking troth
with a damsel of thirty. The real traverser
of the match appears to have been the defend-
ant's housekeeper.

At the Central Criminal Court, Frank
Fisher, who fatally stabbed a fellow workman
in a hat faotory in the Borough, was brought
up for judgment; and Mr. Justice Quain,
giving weight to the strong mitigating circum-
stances in the case, sentenced him to twelve
months' imprisonment with hard labour. In
Mr. Commissioner Kerr's Court, an engineer,
named Frederick Barker, was found guilty of
bigamy, under circumstances which made
his conduct peculiarly heartless and gross,
and received sentence of five years' penal
servitude.

William Lace was executed on Monday
morning in Taunton Gaol for the murder of
his wife. Caloratt was the executioner, and
the prisoner, who has conducted himself well
since his condemnation, and expressed no
desire to live, died almost without a struggle.
The culprit, on the 23rd April, excited by
drink, and by an accusation against his wife,
kicked her 'barbarously for an hour. The
neighbours, to whom she fled, remonstrated,
but did not aotively interfere. When arrested
he acknowledged his guilt, and on his trial, at
the Wells assizes, Mr. Justice Mellor held out
no hope of mercy. A petition for a com-
mutation of sentence, on the ground of
previous good character, was ineffectual.
The couple had lived happily together, and
the children are well provided for.

The Glyncorrwg incline, near Briton Ferry,
has been the scene of another very serious
accident. Several loaded waggons were being
run down the incline, when the steel wire-rope
with which they were worked gave way, and
the result was a terrible smash. No loss of
life is recorded.

A. shocking accident occurred. near Sheffield
on Saturday. Mr. Thompson, who was driving
an omnibus at Abbeydale, loaned over the
" boot " to put on the brake, and. in doing so
fell between the "boot" and the horses. This
frightened the animals, and they started off at
a terrific pace. Mr. Thompson was killed,
having been kicked on the head by the horses
and also been run over by two of the wheels.
Several of the passengers jumped from the
top of the vehicle, and three of them were
seriously injured.

Referring to the Preston election, the Man-
chester Courier says that in the event of there
being a contest, which is very doubtful, the
election will excite an independent interest by
reason of the Ballot Act. It will be the
second contest under that Ad, and will afford
a great deal better idea of the working of the
Ballot than the election of Pontefraot did. The
registered electors number about 11,300, and
about 10,500 voted in 1868. The election is
fixed to take place on Monday, the 9th of
September.

A visitor to the Isle of Man, named
Swindells, fell over the cliff at St. Anne's
Head, near Douglas, on Sunday evening, and
was precipitated a depth of 60 feet upon the
rooks below. He had incautiously approached
the edge of the preeipice above the rifle range,
and the ground being slippery frim the heavy
rain, he fell over. He received dreadful
injuries on the head, and is in a precarious
condition.

At Chatham on Monday two persons were
fined respectively 38s. and 475. (and, in
default, one was sent to prison for fourteen
days), for taking part in a disturbance on
Saturday night, when a mob of some four
hundred persons broke the doors of public-
houses and stoned the police.

The Conseil-General of Rouen have rejected
a motion tending to invite M. niers to that
town. The motives are that they do not wish
to imitate former regimes; nor to deprive M.
Thiers of the time he saves from his recess
for the performance of most arduous and
important duties.

Conscription is dead in Prance, the last
drawing having taken place on Sunday. Many
emigrants from the ceded provinces presented
themselves at the urn.

On Sunday morning the Empress Eugenie
and. the Prince attended High Mass at the
Catholic Church in Cowes, walking through
the streets from the hotel with one or two
attendants. Her Majesty and the Prince were
everywhere received with the most silent and
respectful attention.

The Marquis of Bute, though suffering great
pain from his recent accident, is progressing
favourably.

The Paris Ordre states that "the Emperor
Napoleon has received such a quantity of
letters apropos of the 15th of August, that his
Majesty is obliged to make it known that
several weeks must elapse before he will be
able to reply to all the numerous marks of
sympathy addressed to him."

Much speculation has been excited in Paris
by the arrival there of a Russian diplomatic)
envoy on his way to Trouville. It is esti-
mated that, after seeing M. Thiers, he will
seek an interview with Lord Granville.

Anti-cholera preoautions are being taken at
Copenhagen, with special reference to the trade
coming from the port of Narva.

Among the passengers on board the Cunard
steamer Russia, which left the Mersey on
Saturday for New York, were Baron Leder,
the Austrian Minister, Mr. J. Fielden, M.P.,
and Signor Mario.

A meeting of working men, members of
benefit societies, lodges, and others was held
in Birmingham on Saturday night, when it
was resolved to form an "Anti-Licensing Act
Association," aud a committee was appointed.
Several persons addressed the meeting, urging
the necessity for a respectful public agitation
to be proceeded with, in order to induce the
licensing magistrates to withdraw the restric-
tion placed upon public-houses, by having to
close at 11 o'clock at night.

The Prince of Wales arrived at Dieppe on
Sunday, from Trouville, in the yacht Xantha.
There was no public demonstration. The
Prince did not remain long.

The Justices of Manchester have appointed
a Lioensing Committee of their body under
the Act.

The Bishop of Oxford has determined to
hold a Clerical synod at Oxford, and all the
clergy of the diocese are cited to appear in the
library of Christ Church, on Thursday, the
23rd of October. Among the matters to be
submitted to the synod will be the constitution
of a representative body of the clergy of the
diocese to take part with the laity in a future
diocesan conference.

Captain Black, the Southampton superin-
tendent of the Peninsular and Oriental Com-
pany, has been at Venice to inaugurate the
commencement of the mail steam packet
communication, by ffieaus of that Company's
ships, between Italy and the East. While at
Venice Captain Black received a private letter
from Dr. Livingstone at Ujiji, per favour of
Mr. Stanley, the distinguished American
traveller. Captain Black is an intimate
friend of the illustrious African explorer and
missionary.

The two corporals of Marines (Lynch and
Rogeis) who were recently convicted of taking
part in religious services outside the Ports-
mouth Barraoks, after having been directed
not to do so, have been bought out of the
service. The purchase-money has been lodged
with the authorities this week, and the men
have left the barracks.

A fatal quarrel took place between two men
at Knott Hill, Manchester, on Saturday even-
ing. A man named John Edge struck another
man named Lee. The latter fell to the
ground, and died a few minutes afterwards.

Signor Mario, who with Pauline Lucca and
others, is about to fulfil a professional engage-
ment in America, sailed from Liverpool for
New York on Saturday, in the Canard steamer
Russia.

The Manchester Farmers' Club on Saturday
passed a resolution to the effect that on public
grounds analysts ought to be appointed by
the Corporations of Manchester and Salford.

At the Bridgend Police-court a hawker,
named Thomas Jones, has been committed for
trial to the assizes on a charge of wile murder.

The London and North-Western Railway
Company have commenced surveys for a line
from Beaton to King's Cliff°. The Midland
Railway Company have been surveying for a
new line from KetteOng to Weldon, King's
Cliff°, and StAmford.

AUG. 31, 1872._

The funeral of the Fenian convict Bryan
Dillon was made the occasion of a great
National demonstration at Cork on Sunday.
The procession passed off without disturb"
ance.

Extensive alterations are being made in
the ancient buildings of the Charter House,
especially between the lower end of the
Great Hall and the Preacher's Court.

The Dean of Westminster preached on
Sunday in the Town Church, St. Andrew's.
As far as can be ascertained, Dr. Stanley is the
first Episoopalian dignitary who has officiated
within its preoints since the Revolution of
1688.

The Manchester police have just arrested a
burglar, who drew a revolver and fired at ow)
of the officers, who was wounded. Urn
searching some of the man's luggage the
officers found a large quantity of jewelry and
a complete set of housebreaking instruments)!

In Edinburgh last week, before Shea
Hamilton as commissioner appointed by
.the
"Mixed Commission on British and American
Claims, under the 12th article of the Treaty
of Washington of May 8, 1871," several
witnesses were examined for Messrs. Laurie,
Sons, and Co.; with reference to a claim of
about .t 30,000 at their instance, against the
United States Government. The claim arose
out of a large quantity of tobacco stored ie
several public warehouses in Richmond, which
took fire during the American civil war.

The reports presented to the Metropolitan
Asylums Board show that during the last four
weeks 50 small-pox patients had been received
at Stockwell Hospital, of whom-15 had died;
67 had been discharged. Twelve fever patients
had. been received, of whom three had died
and six had been discharged. At Homerton
there were sto small-pox patients at the date
of last report, and 54 had since been admitted;
44 had been discharged, and 8 had died.
Of the 58 fever patients '25 had been discharged.
and 4 had died. The Caterham Asylum now
contains 1,670 imbecile patients, and the
Leavesden Asylum 1,636 patients.

At the Liverpool Assizes in the ()asp ef
Carey v. Young, the litigants were comedians.
The plaintiff having composed and registered
a song entitled" Mrs. O'Mulligan's Party," the
defendant sang it without permission, and was
therefore sued for a breach of copyright A
verdict was taken for the plaintiff, with leave
to Mr. Young to move the court above on a
point reserved.

The Bellerophon has gone to Portsmouth
harbour to be surveyed, and to have repaired
the damage caused by her collision with the
Minotaur during the recent cruise of the
Channel Squadron.

James Jolliffe, a young man in the empleY
of Mr. William Manfield, Qf Portoham, near
Dorchester, has met his death in rather a
peculiar manner. Deceased was on the top of
a load of wheat preparing to unloesi, wb
suddenly it toppled over. Ile fell with it,
and came in contact with a two-prong fork
with such violence that one of the prongs
penetrated to the heart, killing him on the spot.

The roll of voters for the county of Vin.
burgh for the year ending 1872-73 has just
been completed. It shows a total of 2,60
voters being an Increase of 29 as compared
with the previous year.

The estate of Raavay and Rona, cousistiPg
of the islands of Raasay, Rona Fladda,
was sold in Edinburgh last week. The upset
price was £50,000. Competition was opened,
and went on briskly to £55,000, at which
price the estate fell to Mr. George Mackay, of
Rosehall and Oban.

The Swiss journals announce the inaugura•
tion of an English &lurch at Samaden. Arch-
bishop Anderson officiated, and in a short dis-
course referred in very friendly terms to the
Swiss as a nation, praising their institutions,
especially that of the National Church of the
country.

The Metropolitan Asylums Board agreed 0,11
Saturday to transfer the hospital ship Druca'
nought to the City of London, as the sanitary
authority of that port. Reoommendatione
from the Financial Committee that £12,0
should be raised from the parishes and unienl
of the metropolis for the maintenance 0'
patients, and £41,833 for common 'charge°,
were adopted.

A double inquest was held at Woolwich 03
the bodies of Amelia Hughes, aged twelitYi
and Jacob Whyman, aged twenty-six, °
Canning-town, who were drowned in the
deplorable boat accident off the Southern,
Outfall Sewer Works, Crossness Point, 33'
whose bodies were found together five 4aYO
afterwards off Woolwich. The jury, aitir
hearing the mots, returned a verdict of 00'.
dentally drowned. The young people were
-flgaged to be married.

A great meeting of the inhabitants of Shef-
field was held in Paradise-square on Monday
evening, at which a memorial .to the local
magistrates was unanimously adopted, praying
them to sanction the same hours of opening
and closing public-houses as are in existence
in London.

About thirty persons were on Monday
charged before the Exeter magistrates with
having participated in the recent riots in that
city. Several of the defendants were sum-
marily dealt with, but the majority were
bound over to appear at the Quarter Sessions.

The inquest upon the body of Hermann
Nagel, the victim of the Chelsea tragedy, was
resumed on Monday before Dr. Diplook, when
the evidence of Ellen Gordon, the servant,
the interpreter, and Dr. Godrich was taken.
The deposition of the survivor, Paul May, was
also read. After Augusta Burgess had been
recalled and questioned, the inquiry was again
adjourned until Thursday.

At the Clerkenwell Police-court on Monday
a costermonger, Edward M'Carthy by name,
was convicted of having violently assaulted
two policemen. He was sontenoed to three
months' imprisonment with hard labour. At
Worship-street there were several cases of a
like character, and sentences varying from
seven days to two months' imprisonment were
passed. Similar sentences were passed at the
Southwark and Thames courts.

In opening the National Exhibition of Art
at Milan on Monday, amid gratifying de-
monstrations of loyalty, the King of Italy
remarked that the common country of those
assembled was progressing in everything that
tended to promote its real happiness and
prosperity.

A telegram from Madrid states that the
lilinistorial candidates have been successful in
all the electoral bureaux of Madrid. It is
reported that the radicals are supporting the
Government.

It is announced by telegram from Berlin
that the festivities on the occasion of the
impending visit of the Emperors of
Austria and Russia will open on the
principal day—the 7th of September—with a
grand parade of troops in the forenoon. in the
afternoon the Emperor William will entertain
• his Imperial guests at a banquet at the Royal
Castle, and in the evening there will be a gala
performance at the Opera, and the whole city
will be illuminated.

Another violent thunderstorm passed over a
part of Leicestershire on Tuesday, and several
houses were struck by lightning.

According to the return of the Registrar-
General, the mean temperature of the air at
the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, was 64
deg. 3 min. last week, and 3 deg. 6 niin, above
the average for the corresponding week in
fifty years. An excess prevailed on each day
of the week, and amounted to 6 deg. 5 min.
on Wednesday, when the mean was 67 deg. 2
mm.; on Saturclay`the mean fell to GO deg. 8
min.

Further intelligence is brought by the West
India mail respecting the revolution in Peru.
It appears that Congress declared Colonel
Gutierrez an outlaw, and that the Diplomatic
Corps refused to recognise him as President.
The army was every moment being diminished
by desertions, and the navy stood out to sea;
the banks and commercial establishments were
all dosed. Mr. Dawson, the manager of the
London Bank, was kept a prisoner until ho
granted a loan. The brother of Gutierrez
having been killed by opponents of the
usurper, the latter despatched orders to kill
President Balta. He was shot while lying ill
in bed, and his body pierced with bayonets.
Gutierrez himself was afterwards killed in a
druggist's shop, where he had taken refuge
from a crowd, and the naked corpses of
Gutierrez and two of his brothers were first
hung to a lamp-post, then hoisted by pulleys
to the tower of the Lima Cathedral, and
afterwards rubbed with kerosene and burnt in
the public market-place. The dictatorship
lasted about four days.

A correspondent at Brussels furnishes ad-
ditional particulars respecting the Scientific
Congress in that city, and its researches into
traces of primitive and pro-historic man.

A flatman, named John Martin, has found
the body of apparently a boatman, about
fifty years of age, floating in the river opposite
Egremont Ferry. There are some cuts and
other marks of violence on the head, and
what gives the matter a very suwicious
appearanee is the fact that both legs were tied
at the knees with a thick rope. This circum-
stance has created a suppositioa that the
deces.E.ed must have met with foulTlay. The
letters " S.E." are marked in Indian ink on
the left arm. The body is dressed in blue
cloth trousers, a grey corded vest, and a blue
and white linen shirt. The deceased was a
stoutly-built man, and his head bald.

The number of visitors admitted to the In-
ternational Exhibition last week was as fol-
lows :--Season tiekets,l,9lB ; on payment of
2s. 6d. 986; ditto is. ; 20,955 ; total 23,869.

The freedom of Kirkwall was presented to
Mr. Lowe on Saturday., He is said to have
made a humorous speech. Mr. Lowe visited
the town with Mr. Pender, M.P., and Lord
John Hay. The party were shown the Cathe-
dral and other objects of interest. In the
afternoon the members of the Council and
others took luncheon on board Mr. Bender's
yacht, which in the course of the evening
sailed for Skye.

The market train from Llanberis to Car-
narvon, whilst approaching the latter town
on Saturday, was run into by a ballast
engine. A second-class carriage was knocked
to pieces, the two passengers it contained
having a miraculous escape. The carriages
behind were also damaged, and the passengers
were violently shaken.

The herring fishery on the North-Eastern
Coast is reported to be very inferior, the
majority of the boats taking almost nothing.

Mr. F. Perkins is a candidate for the
vacancy in Coleman-street Ward, occasioned
by the death of Mr. Alderman Hale.

Two sham French Communists were on
Monday convicted at the Greenwich Police
Court of having obtained alms under false
pretences, and each of them was sent to
Maidstone Gaol for a month, with hard
labour.

On. Monday the August Sessions of the
Central Criminal Court were brought to a close.
In the ease of Catherine Alice Kinnear, whose
trial on a charge of perjury had reached the
third day, the jury after a deliberation of half
an hour, returned. into Court with a verdict of
Not Guilty.

Two charges of assaulting children were
investigated before Metropolitan police magis-
trates on Monday. At flow-street the de-
fendant was one Daniel Lowe, twenty-nine
years of age, and described as a porter. He
had severely beaten his stepdaughter, a little
girl of nine, and was sent to prison for four
months with hard labour.—At Marylebone
Henry Brown, a labourer, was charged with
having severely thrashed his daughter, 13
years of age. .His defence was that a pair of
black eyes and a bruised countenance were to
be regarded in the light of correctives. He
was remanded.

A Penrith labourer named Wilkinson, who
is described as having been in a continual
state of intoxication, on Tuesday made an
attempt upon the life of his wife as well as
upon his own. Wilkinson is in custody.

At the meeting of the Liverpool Presbytery of
the English Presbyterib.n Church, on Monday,
a resolution was unanimously adopted to me.
morialise the local authorities in favour of
the reduction of the hours of sale of liquor on
Sundays to the minimum specified by the new
Act.

There was an extraordinary personal alterca-
tion at the Brewster Sessions, at Norwich, on
Tuesday. In the course of the proceedings
some unpleasant feeling arose between Dir.
Wiffen Blake and Captain Bignold. The
gallant officer called Mr. Blake a foolish old
man. Mr. Blake then struck him, and the
pair ultimately rolled on the floor struggling
together, The scene, of course, produced
much exltement among the auditory. Even-
tually the combatants were separated.

The early closing movement seems to be
fast gaining ground on the southern side of
the Thames. Here and there in that district
some firms have adopted it for years; but
now, from the announcement put forth by the
South London Drapers' Association, its adop-
tion appears to have become general. That
announcement states that on and after the 2nd
Sepetmber next the drapers, &e., over the
whole of South London, have resolved to close
their shops at an earlier hour than hitherto,
and that the maximum time fixed for closing
them has been 8 o'clock p.m. and 10 o'clock
on Saturdays all the year round, thus leaving
firms to fix any hour they choose under that
maximum. It has also been intimated that as
a considerable number of firms have already
and for some time closed their places of
business at hours earlier than even those
specified, such firms will still adhere to the
hours they have already fixed.

At the late Middleton Cheney Petty Ses-
sions, Francis Spiers, an innkeeper, at Charlton,
Northamptonshire, was charged with unlaw-
fully smoking on the Great Western Railway
at Banbury, and also with annoying the pas-
sengers with obscene language. The Bench
inflicted the lull penalties of 40s. in each case,
and the expenses, amounting in all to £6 10s.
Monday was the annual licensing clay, and as
Spiers holds a certificate from the Bench, they
deol ned to ienew it.

During the week ending Saturday last
5,007 births and 3,417 births were registered
in London and twenty other large cities and
towns of the United Kingdom. The mor-
tality from all causes was at the rate of 24
deaths annually to every 1,000 persons esti-
mated to be living. In the metropolis 2,089
births and 1,247 deaths were registered, the
former having been 110, and the latter 247
below the average. Fifteen persons died. from
small-pox, 12 from measles, 12 from scarlet
fever, 3 from diphtheria, 35 from whooping
cough, 25 from different forms of fever, and
197 from diarrhcea. The fatal cases of each of
these seven were below the corrected average
numbers in the corresponding week of the last
ten years. The mortality from diarrlicea
showdd a considerable further decrease. To
cholera or choleraic diarrhon twelve deaths
were referred.

The penalty named in [the Licensing Act
for a,second conviction for drunkenness was
imposed on Tuesday at the Wandsworth Police-
court. A woman who had been incapably in-
toxicated twice within a week was ordered to
pay 10s., with the alternative of 14 days' im-
prisonment.

A. sad story of alleged neglect on the part
of parents was told to the Wandsworth police
magistrate on Tuesday. The defendant was
a City clerk named Corrie, at a salary of £2
per week, and the condition of his children,
who are now in the workhouse, was described
at length. In consequence of the absence of
a material witness an adjournment was ordered,
and a surety was required for the attendance
of the defendant.

A boat, containing six factory workmen,
has been out in two by the steamer Palmerston
off Woolwich, and three of the men were
drowned.

During a heavy gale which visited the east
coast on Tuesday the yacht Stella, at anchor
in Holkam Bay, was observed to be making
signals of distress. One of the lifeboats of the
National institution rescued those on board,
one of whom was the Hon. F. Walpole, M.P.
for North Norfolk.

From April Ist to the 24th instant the Ex-
chequer receipts amounted to £27,083,725, as
compared with £24,999,804 in the corres-
ponding period of last year. The expenditure
has been £29,672,195. On Saturday last the
balance in the Bank of England exceeded four
millions sterling.

At the last sitting of the county magistrates
at Halifax, two boys, named William Itawnsley
and Francis Pinder, both under 12 years of
age, were charged with having broken into a
dwelling-house at Barkisland on the previous
Sunday forenoon, and stolen therefrom two
silver watches. The prisoners had a.,scertained
that the door-key was left under a stone near
the door. The property was valued at £B, and
prisoners had hid the articles in a wood.
Both pleaded guilty, and they were ordered to
receive twelve lashes each with a birch rod,
the punishment being awarded to them after
the court had closed.

Colonel H. F. Ponsonby, Private Secretary
to her Majesty, is gazetted to the disti notion
of 0.13.

Captain Shaw's report of a fire at tho
Kentish Town Station of the North London
Railway shows that it was of a very de-
structive character. About 230 feet of the
arrival platform, four waiting rooms, and a
signal box, were destroyed, and many of the
adjacent buildings were more or less damaged.

The body of Mr. Henry Lynch, a Liverpool
solicitor, who mysteriotoly disappeared about
a month ago, was found on Sunday in a ditch
at Lydiate, near Brinskirk.- The deceased was
last seen walking in the neighbourhood of
Lydiate, and it is supposed that during the
night he fell into the ditch and was drowned.
When found the body was so far decomposed
as to be quite unrecognisable except by the
clothes.

On Tuesday Dr. Hardwick° held an inquest
on Mrs. Mary Brown,. widow. She was an
aged lady, residing with her married daughter
in Frome-street. On Friday, when sitting in
the garden, she complained of the excessive
heat of the sun, which she said was scorching
her brain. She was taken into the house and
'provided with a cup of tea. A medical man
was sent for, but before he arrived she died.
The coroner did not consider hot tea was of
much use in a case of sunstroke. The jury
returned a verdict of "Death from sun-
stroke."

'At the Clerkenwell Police-court on Tuesday
a man named ltadley, 34 years of age, was
charged with having attempted to murder his
wife, There had been a disagreement respect-
ing the presence of the Wile's mother in the
house, but it was not of such a character as to
lead the family to suppose that it would result
in the act of violence for which he had been
arrested. A remand was granted.

articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.
In the Court of Bankruptcy yesterday,
before Mr. Registrar /Italia, a meeting was
held in the matter of Algernon Samuel Tom-
king, who is described as a clerk in holy orders,
of 16, St. Mary's-road, Westbourne Park, late
curate of St. Peter's. No statement of no
counts has been filed. The debts are esti-
mated at about £750. The petition in bank_
ruptey was filed' the 30th of July last, adjudi-
cation following on the 12th August. Credi-
tors to the amount of £240 attended and
proved their debts. Resolutions were come
to by which it was agreed to appoint a trustee
and committee of inspection. His Honour
confirmed the appointment.
The explosion which took place in the
drying room at a dyeworks in Manchester,
on Tuesday, has terminated fatally in the
cases of two boys.

Demonstrations in France on the anniver-
saryof the downfall of the Empire have been
officially prohibited.
A collision took place at Preston Railway
Station on Wednesday between two goods
trains, by which several men were injured.
A fire took place on Wednesday night at a
house in Temperley-road, Balham-hill, the
residence of Mr. J. Eastlake, in consequence of
an escape of gas. The front of the house and
its contents were severely Niamaged by the
explosion and by fire, and three persons were
slightly burnt on the hands and face.
The crew of the fishing lugger York, who
it was feared had been lost by the collision on
Tuesday between their vessel and the sloop
Bottle Imp, have been picked up by a Lowe-
stoft boat and taken into that port. The York
was lost.

John Cox, the collector of the Kentish' and
Camden-towns Volunteer Fire Brigade, was
charged before Mr. D'Eyncourt at Marylebone
Police Court yesterday with being drunk and
violently assaulting Mr. Edmund Reanay, the
superintendent of the brigade. The defendant
said he was very sorry, but would leave if Mr.
Reanay would pay what was due to him. Mr.
D'Eynoourt said the defendant's conduct was
very bad, and ordered him to pay a fine of 405.,
or to be imprisoned for one month.
Cholera has broken out in a severe form at
Meeanmeer, Lahore, Kassowlio, and elsewhere.
At Meeanmeer 70 men of the 37th Regiment
died. At Lahore there were 200 cases, more
than half of them fatal. The attacks were
sudden and alarming. Dengue fever has
abated in Calcutta, but is still severe in the
other Presidencies. In Madras the 'disease is
intense, and prayers for its abatement are
offered in the churches.

Frances Charlotte Field, of Norbiton, was
charged at the Kingston Petty Sessions on
Wednesday with wilfully neglecting to pro-
vide adequate support for her child, about
four months old. The child was found up.
parently in a starving state, and had been
wasting away from want of nutrition, bad
treatment, and neglect for a considerable time.
Its life was still in danger. The prisoner was
remanded.

Jonathan Hawley, a valet, on Wednesday
*as fined 10s. and costs at Hampstead for
having, whilst suffering from small-pox,
entered a hackney carriage without previously
telling the driver that he was so suffering.
A girl named Margaret Kelly was com-
mitted for trial at Worship-street for the man.
slaughter of Ann Sullivan. There had been
a quarrel between the prisoner and the
deceased, and on the 16th inst. the prisoner
caught the deceased by the hair, threw her
down, and struck her in the head, inflicting a
wound which resulted in her death.

Two girls called at the police-office, Dews-
bury, on Tuesday afternoon, and reported that
a few hours previously they had seen a man
commit suicide. The story they tell is that
the individual was under the influence of
liquor, and they saw him leave a public-house
in Ravensthoree and walk down to the river
aide and jump in In the evening the river was
dragged, but no trace of the man could be
discovered.

Senor Olozaga, the Spanish Minister, intends
to pay a visit to the President of the Republic
at Trouville, and to thank him in the name of
the King of Spain for the friendly assurances
,which the President conveyed to the King
upon the occasion of his journey to San Sebas-
tian,

The Empress Charlotte of Mexico is now
lying in delirious agony, during which she
sometimes is heard to whisper the words,
" Mother," " Victor," " Parts," "
The Archbishop of Malines does not leave her
bedside, in hopes of cheering the last moments
of the victim of the Mexican tragedy. The
King of the Belgians will probably ho
.pre-
vented from taking his usual autumn trip to
England through tho impending death of his
sister.

The eminent historian of the Reformation,
Dr. Merle d'Aubigne, has addressed a letter
of sympathy to Mr. Downton, English chaplain
at Geneva, from his summer retreat in the
highlands of Vaud.

THE ATHANASIAN CREED.
To the Editor of the BEE-HITE.

Sni,—lt is now admitted, even by bishops,
if the people's belief in this Creed was dependent
upon good and satisfaotory evidence being
given of its having been written by A tha-
nasius, that the Christian Evidence Society
could not give evidence shewing that the
Church had authority for asserting it to have
been written by Athana.sius. So that in the
absence of any satisfactory evidence as to who
was the writer of the
,Creed, it ceases to be of
any value to the people, except so far as the
subject-matter of the Creed, and its treatment
thereof comes within the grasp of the people's
understanding to comprehend and receive.
But the subject-matter of the Creed is
treated in such a mystical manner as to be
wholly inexplicable and incomprehensible to
the mind of the people; so that it is wholly
beyond their reason to understand that there
Is any necessity whatever for their making
profession of believing a Creed which they can
neither understand to be good, nor even know
to be true. _ _

And as the' people reject the Creed because
It is not only destitute of "authority," but is
also incomprehensible and inexpheable as
good, therefore the people, in rejecting this
Creed, are innocent of rejecting any revela-
tion, or showing any contempt of God.
And yet we are asked to believe, on the
authority of Dr. Pusey (see Times, 13th inst.)
that a people who obeyed God's command
ments, but rejected this Creed, would be
showing God more contempt than a people
who disobeyed God's conamandraents but
accepted this Creed.
So, notwithstanding that this Creed is a
base forgery, we nevertheless are asked to be-
lieve, on the authority of Dr. Pusey, the
leader of the Ritualists, that the rejecting of
this Creed is a much greater contempt of God
than the disobeying of what God commands.
And, therefore, according to the authority
of Dr. Pusey, the accepting of this Creed is a
far greater merit than obeying God's com-
mands. Ana this teaching scents to agree
exactly with the recorded teaching of Satan
i
—"Worship me, and the world s yours."
But urely we are not going to be the abject
slaves of blind authority, under the fear of
empty anathemas ? T. G. HEADLEY.
• Petersham, S.W.

POVERTY, CRIME, AND EMIGRATION.

To the Editor C)f the BEE-HIVE.

Stn,—Supplementary, perhaps, to every
proposed system of society might, with advan-
tage, appear special schemes tor dealing with
the poverty and crime of a country.
At the present moment, to say the least, we
do not seem to manage these affairs very'
creditably, inasmuch as the great principle
which might, and which, perhaps, ought to
have been the guiding star of all our legisla-
tion on thd subject, seems to have been
utterly ignored in our ordinary measures in
connection with it; and thus poverty and
crime, instead of being made always to bear
their own expenses, have been allowed to con-
stitute a perpetual and really grievous burden
on the more provident and better disposed
portions of the community.
Nor is this all of our folly in the case. In
addition to our " muddle " of such topics, we
have, forsooth, been promoting emigration—
emigration, too, of that special tissue of
simplicity which, keeping our rogues, vaga-
bonds, and incompetents of all kinds at home,
or, in certain even of the worst cases, philan-
thropically providing them almost contem-
poraneously with their lied migrare, with
sympathetic tickets-of-leave to return as early
its possible,when , by any miscarriage ofour good
intentions, they have really (temporarily) gone,
sends on the contrary from our shores in all
hot haste, with even assisted passages—a new
Israel from a modern Egypt—men who re-
maining might possibly, have ultimately con-
stituted to us much of our honour, strength,
and comeliness in the presence of the sister
nations of the world.
Now, I hold that neither proverty, nor crime,
nor the emigrational, remedial, or custodial
expenses connected with either, ought to cost
the country anything. Further, I cannot but
hink that incompetency or crime, espeoially
the latter, once banished ought for ever to be
banished; the judicial hand of the country,
moreover, though ever tempering its rule
with Christian mercy, never altogether fore-
going its hold on either of those two great
living barriers to the human progress—the
pauper and the criminal. Finally, were our
civilization higher, international arrangements
with respect to both might, perhaps, be
made with advantage, pecuniary or other-
wise, to all the nations concerned in their
construction. Meanwhile, governments should,
think, reward as well as punish men
who have already well night breathed
their share of this world's airs, or fully wrought

their share of its toils, ought not in their old
age, after an honourable and even if humble,
a duly certificated career, during which,
doubtless, they have always produced for
society far more than they have consumed.
Snell men, I say, whether disabled at last
either by age, or by any of the common mishaps
of life, ought never to be utterly neglected or
disregarded, and no teachings of the political
economist should ever induce a Christian
people to forget the plain and obvious duty it
owes to them. National benevolence largely,
not private benevolence, necessarily on a
niggard s3ale should be the effective agent
employed in dealing with their case.
Reservin g any practical suggestions, however,
as to either of the topics above touched upon
to a future letter, and regretting that recent
congresses, in connection with more than one
of such Important subjeots have elicited
nothing apparently in permanent settlement of
such constantly vexed questions,—l am, Sir,
&c.,
W. A. RUSSELL.
Collegiate School, Greenwich.

EMIeRATION.
To the Editk of the BnE-HivE,

Sia,—lt is a disadvantage to the working
man in England, as compared with his fellows
in America, that his " West " is separated from
him by the ocean. This disadvantage, how-
ever, is growing less, the means of transit
becoming easier every day.
It is the want of trustworthy information
regarding the thinly-peopled portions of the
earth, rather than the difficulties of reaching
them which, very properly, deters men who
find it difficult to earn their living in England
from seeking their fortunes abroad. I think,
therefore, that every trade union should have
its corresponding members, if not in one of
our own colonies, at least in what were once
our colonies, whose inhabitants, therefore,
speak the same language, and live under
almost the same laws as ourselves. _

I know nothing more dastardly than
the attempts by capitalists to inveigle
working men from England, to countries
in which field labour is to them impos-
sible, except with a very great waste of
life; it is a crime ' little less atrocious
than kidnapping South Sea Islanders. I
would advise working men to trust none but
working men who are known to them in this
matter of choosing a new country. And it is
for this reason that I suggest that every trade
should have its own corresponding members in
the colonies. s I would especially warn work-
ing men against accepting assisted emigration
to latitudes within forty degrees of the equator,
except as miners in mountainous regions.
Once landed in these countries in debt, they
are almost hopelessly enslaved, and even if for-
tunate enough to work out their own freedom,
they arc still, if they have families dependent
upon them, unable to escape.
Emigration is the only way by which the
right balance between numbers and the means
of subsistence can be kept in adjustment.
Emigration should, however, not be a hurried
remedy, not a drastic purge against reple-
tion, but a simple alterative, by which a
healthy action in the body politic is preserved.
Co-operation is for emigration the proper mode
of action—a co-operation stretching across the
Atlantic, so that emigrants on reaching their
destination would be received by members of
their own society, in which they would have
the same status as in the parent society to
which they belonged before lea.vin_g England.
O —Your obedient servant, MICRON.
August 26th.

GLASS BOTTLE MAKERS' OF
GREAT BRITAIN AND IH,EL A.ND
AMALGAMATED TRADE ASSOCIA.
TION.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SlR,—it is now twenty-seven weeks since
the commencement of a strike in the Glasgow
district of the above association, and at the
present time there are no apparent signs of a
settlement; but notwithstanding the length of
time this struggle has lasted, there is a
prospect of a satisfactory result, and at • a
general meeting held on Monday last, August
19, it was resolved that the men should hold
out firmly until their demand wasgranted, and
not to deviate the least from the original
demands.

Hitherto the contest on the part of the men
has been conducted with a good spirit and with
great moderation and precaution; and up to
the present time the spirit of unity has been
so well manifested that not one man has
betrayed his fellow man.
So far as the " demands " are concerned,
they are unquestionably reasonable,
.judging
from this simple fad---the masters have not
themselves pointed out their unreasonable-
ness or their impracticability. And it has long
been a settled question with us that this con-
flict is being carried on against us on un-
principled grounds, and with the hostile
feelings such as have been exhibited only in a
few instances during the List two years. In
other words, it is quite clear that the Only
object of our employers is to break up our
union, and.thus prevent us from having a fair
remuneration for our labour, and, what i still

more important, subject us to their tyrannous
oppressions; but, thanks to our fellow trades-
,men. in England and Ireland, a few other
sympathising. trade unionists we have been
enabled to stand the test, and we have a hope
yet to see right triumph over might.
On several occasions we have endeavoured to
have a
.conference with the masters, but we
were successful only in one instance, .and
through the extreme obstinacy of the masters
the meeting separated without making the
least approach to a settlement. At that same
meeting one of their number estimated that
now they had an association composed of all
the manufacturers of Scotland with one ex-
*coption, and yet this same gentleman declined
to acknowledge a letter from Our committee
this week, because, as he states, it was signed
by the secretary, and he intimated that he
desired to make his bargain with his own
men.

This, Sir, to say the least, is very erro-
neous. Up to the time of this dispute each
firm had its own separate regulations, and I
may say it is scarcely possible to frame rules
more stringent than those the bottle makers
of Scotland were subjected to. No man was
expected to dissent or object to the regulations.
If by chance a man ventured to raise his voice,
he was speedily informed "if you are not
satisfied, you can leave."
Several attempts were made to mend matters
but to no purpose, until in February last, the
men resolved to make a decided stand; hence
this protracted struggle. Many of our men
have suffered great hardships, but to-day they
are just as determined to gain the victory as
they were six months ago. They have resolved
to have a code of working rules, by which the
hours of labour, wages, and all other terms
and conditions shall be fully and fairly set
forth, and signed by responsible parties on
behalf of workmen and masters, with a regula-
tion to the effect that three months' notice must
be given by either party before any alteration
can be agreed to, as it is very desirous that we
should, as far as practicable, prevent a re-
occurrence of these disastrous strikes.—l am,
respectifully yours,
C. BISHOP, General Secretary.
Glasgow, August 24th, 1872.

THE FABULOUS WEALTH OF
• FRANCE AND THE NEW LOAN.
To the Editor of the 'BEE-TIIVE.

SIR,—I think you would be doing good
service if you were to give your readers a
caution on the subject of certain fallacies that
are now largely promulgated by our Liberal
journals in their articles on the new French
.Loan. When I find them writing in glowing
terms of the fabulous wealth of France, it has
repeatedly struck me that, without exactly
intending it, they have chosen a very proper
epithet. I greatly fear that investors will find
to their cost that their chance of repayment is
indeed fabulous. When we consider that it
but three-quarters of a century since France was
bankrupt, and her Assignats could be bought
by the bushel as waste paper, and when we
further consider that i no one year during
the present century she has over been able to
mako the ends or the year meet without
borrowing more money, the confidence so loudly
expressed, in her ability and willingness to
bear the enormous additional weight about to
be. imposed upon her appears to me to be
almost incomprehensible.
If France during the comparatively pros-
perous reign of Louis Phillippe, with a smaller
army and navy than she now has, and without
a single foreign war during the whole eighteen
years, nevertheless doubled her debt, how
comes it that now, when she has lost some of
her most valuable provinces, and again more
than doubled her debt, and suffered the
greatest reverses recorded in modern history,
she should be able to issue the largest national
loan on record, on more favourable terms
than formerly? . •
America, after her low, and expensive civil
war, rapidly recovered her credit;- but in her
ease the explanation is obvious: she imme-
diately reduced her army and navy, imposed
heavy taxes, raised a large surplus revenue,
and. honourably began to discharge her debts.
Had France imitated the wise and noble con-
duct of America, she might 'have deserved the
confidence now demanded for her; but unfor-
tunately her conduct has been precisely the
reverse. She has increased her anny,increased
her expenditure, and squabbled over the sub-
ject of taxation; with no other prospect in the
future than a continuance of annual de.fleits.
Her present ruler declares that there is no
other possible way of increasing the national
income than by imposing taxes upon raw
materials. Now let me beg of your readers to
consider attentively what this means. It will
be admitted on all hands that France cannot
retain her rank amongst nations without
her foreign commerce; it must also be
admitted that her merchants cannot sell her
manufactures • to foreign nations unless they
can compete with the manufactures of England
and Belgium; therefore if the raw materials of
those manufactures are taxed, there is only
one way in which this can be accomplished,
and that is by a reduction of wages.
The two great items in the price of manu-
factured goods are the cost of raw material,
and the cost of labour. Now if the French

AUG. 31, 187.2._

manufacturer is compelled to pay more for
the raw material than the English or the Bel-
gian manufacturer has to pay, and in order to
get foreign customers he must sell his goods at
as low a price as they do. There is no possible
means by which he can be enabled to do this
except by cutting down the wages of the
workmen. If we consider how theroughlY
the working men of France are alive to the
importance of this question of taxation, which
is now so eagerly discussed in every greet
town of France, I feel satisfied that should AL
niers be able to carry his iniquitous scheme,
it must be followed, at no distant date, by
general insurrection.
Had the much-abused Commune been suc•-
cessful, France might have escaped thie
danger. Their proposal to pay off the Ger-
man indemnity by means of a property tog
spread over a certain number of years was a
far more wise, honest, and statesmanlike
measure than any that has been proposed by
the Assembly at Versailles. Had such a tax
been accompanied by a resolute reduction of
the army and navy, there would have then
been a fair opportunity for the talent and in-
dustry of France to have restored her general
prosperity. As it is, I see no escape from
bankruptcy on the one baud, or a fresh re-
volution on the other.—l have the honour to
be, sir, yours respectfully,
J. GrRNEY Bina.
Crown Villas, Lee, Kent.

THE MASONS AND JOINERS..
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Sit,—As a reader of your valuable paper, I
have read a letter from William Graham on the
dispute now going on in the London building
trades, and, as one that cannot agree 'with the
view ho takes upon it, I will try and be as
brief as possible. Now, Sir, he seems to
think that the difference between the masons
and the joiners is one of trades unionism. I
beg leave to tell him that it is one of principle,
the one trade becoming traitors to the other.
It was generally understood between the two
trades that there was a mutual agreement
between them—whatever step the one might
take they would let it be known to the other.
Now, let us see what the -delegates of the
carpenters did do. At any time that they
agreed to appoint a deputation to wait upon
the employers it was always known by the
masons; if they did not get it officially they
got it semi-officially through the press, the
reporters beieg always present at our meetings.
Now, let us turn to the masons, and take a
review of their conduct. They held a secret
meeting of the officials of their trade society,
and agreed to appoint a deputation with full
power to settle the dispute concerning their
trade, and this was done without the sanction
of the general body of their own trade. Now
I don't deny them the right to settle the dis-
pute concerning themselves, if their trade
agrees to the terms which they came to with the
employers; but Mr. Broadhurst did not think
it worth the trouble to make the Central Com-
mittee of the Carpenters and Joiners aware of
the step they had taken until they, had,
been before the employers, and come to an
agreement with them. Now, Sir, it is gene-
rally believed, by the action that the masons
took on that occasion, it has been the means
of dragging us into a long struggle; it was the
means of shaking the confidence of the men
in giving power to any deputation to settle
the dispute on their behalf at that time ; but
now,when they find that there are men amongst
them that are above suspicion, they have con-
ceded to give them fdill power to act on their
behalf by appointing the committee in con-
junction with a limited number of the dele-
gates. Now, Sir, I am convinced this step
would have been taken five weeks ago, if it
had not been for the way that Mr. Broadhurst
and his colleagues have acted.
As regards the latter portion of your corre-
spondent's letter, I will say that at all the
delegates' meetings I have attended, I have
never yet heard an ill word said against
yourself, or Mr. Applegarth, or Mr. Cremer ;
but, Sir, it is very well known that there is a
degree of animus between those two gentlemen,
that if they had been called in to give us
counsel that they would have been the meting
of breaking us up in two sections.
Hoping you will find room to insert the
above in the columns of the BEE-HIVE in your
next you will greatly oblige.—l am, Sir, yours
truly,

A. SCOTT, Joiner.

THE RAILWAY SERVANTS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Slß,—Since the agitation among railwat
servants first commenced, many and various
improvements have been effected; but there
remains many more yet to be obtained, and
have no doubt that, with proper organisation
and actomplished officers, comparative if not
complete success. will ere long be the result.
Unfortunately the North- Western
goo
porters have allowed themselves to be so far
misled by reckless individuals as to strike,
in order to procure a certain officer's dismissal.
I am sorry for this, both for the men's own
interest and because it has considerably
checked the progress of their soeiety—the
Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants.
A. moment's consideration would, I think, have
ds

told these men that they could not pos-
sibly have succeeded against a powerful
company like the North-Western, unless, in-
deed, they had got other classes to have gone
out with them, which was not for a moment
to be expected, as the individual in question
had no power or control over any but the
goods porters, and, therefore, had not made
himself obnoxious to any other class.
The president of the any
Society
has since wrote to what the men call—but
what I have some misgivings about—the
" guardian of their interests," stating that the
North-Western men did not strike to procure
their superintendent's dismissal, only for his
removal. I think he had better not have done
this, as it proves that the men care but very
little as to who was troubled or plagued with
this now notorious officers° long as they were
not.

With respect to strikes among railway ser-
vants, my impression is that they will seldom,
if ever, succeed. Their conditions and pros-
pects arc too various for there to be that unity
among them which is absolutely necessary for
the success of a strike. •

. •
It can hardly be supposed that the man
who receives eight shillings a day will strike
because another one only receives two shil-
lings, or that he who works only eight hours a
day will do oo because another one works
double the number. As to going out on strike
for procuring the dismissal of obnoxious
officials all I can say is, that if the men suc-
ceed, the companies too will succeed.
To the companies it will be—" the loss of
one is the choice of plenty more," of a similar
typo.
• My conviction, therefore, is that railway
men, being public servants, ,cannot do better
than to appeal to the public. This they can
